summary: Mine real niche subcultures for pain points, generate non-obvious ideas using 1+ sponsor, kill anything Claude-default

top5.name: Meta Lock
top5.one_liner: A puzzle hunt where the prize money sits in a wallet whose password is the final puzzle's answer. The first team to really solve it takes the money themselves, with no judge and no answer server.
top5.the_story: Small online puzzle hunts are run by volunteers. They keep a table of answers on one server, which leaks to testers and crashes at kickoff, and then someone has to stay up to confirm the winner and send the prize. Meta Lock turns each answer into a wallet key, so typing the right answer is the answer check and the prize claim at the same time. The hunt's server stores zero answers.
top5.insider_detail: Hunt answers are already cleaned up to plain capital letters ('Pickle-ball!' becomes PICKLEBALL), so an answer works as a key seed with no extra rules. Hunts already invent their own hint currencies, like GPH's 'advicebergs'. Since 2009 the MIT Hunt keeps running after the coin is found, so 'someone won' and 'everyone keeps solving' have to work side by side.
top5.sponsor_use: XRPL is the whole idea. The key is derived from scrypt(ANSWER + a salt published at kickoff). Each puzzle publishes only its address, and the browser checks answers locally by comparing addresses. A solve is a signature tied to the team, so another team can't replay it. Hint currency is an MPT, and the meta wallet holding the pot is swept by whoever solves it. A Credential 'SOLVED: META' goes to the winners. No other sponsor is needed.
top5.demo_moment: A wrong answer does nothing and makes no network call. 'PICKLEBALL' makes the hint balance tick up on-ledger. Typing the meta answer moves the pot out of the answer wallet on the testnet explorer within about 4 seconds. Then we open the hunt's database and show it's empty.
top5.real_vs_mocked: Real: key derivation, the local checker, the signed solve relay, MPT hint tokens, the pot sweep and the Credential, plus 3-4 real mini-puzzles. Mocked: nothing that matters. Run it as a live mini-hunt at the hackathon with a small real testnet pot for social proof.
top5.originality_score: 9/10. A brain-wallet is an old crypto idea, but making the puzzle's answer literally unlock the prize, and deleting the answer server, is something I haven't seen. A default brainstorm gives 'NFT for solvers' or 'pay for hints'.
top5.buildability_score: 9/10. It's all xrpl.js plus scrypt and a static site. The hardest part is writing good puzzles.
top5.biggest_risk: Brute force. Answers are dictionary words, so it needs a kickoff-only salt, slow scrypt settings and a small pot. Say this out loud in the pitch.

top5.name: Countermark
top5.one_liner: A pigeon-race clock nobody owns: each bird carries a secret code on its leg, and typing that code in when it lands is what stops the clock on the blockchain.
top5.the_story: A club race secretary has to settle 2-second disputes between members using sealed mechanical clocks and a secret list of ring numbers he keeps in a drawer, and everyone suspects him. Race clocks also come from a short list of approved vendors. Countermark commits each bird's secret code on-ledger before release. When the bird lands, the owner types the code from its leg, and the ledger timestamp becomes the official arrival time.
top5.insider_detail: Pigeon clocking has been a commit-reveal scheme for about 100 years. Each bird gets a numbered rubber 'countermark' ring that the club records in secret. The owner pulls it off the returning bird and drops it into the sealed clock. A preimage escrow is the same thing in cryptographic form. The ranking metric is velocity (yards per minute from the surveyed distance), so the timestamps are everything.
top5.sponsor_use: Each bird gets an XRPL escrow with Condition = hash(countermark) and CancelAfter = race close. Finishing it is the clocking, and the ledger time is the arrival. Escrows for birds that never come home cancel on their own, which gives a public lost-birds list. The release point gets a memo tx, optionally signed by a multisig committee. Batch pays out prizes. ElevenLabs does the 'loft radio' bonus.
top5.demo_moment: A teammate walks in with a stuffed pigeon wearing a paper leg band and types the code. The leaderboard reorders, the EscrowFinish shows up on the explorer, and a radio voice reads out '1,412 yards per minute, provisional first.' At race close, the escrow for the bird the hawk got cancels back.
top5.real_vs_mocked: Real: crypto-condition escrows, the release memo, haversine velocity from real coordinates (Sacramento release to Bay Area lofts), the live ranking and the payout. Mocked: about 20 bot birds arriving on a scripted curve, plus one live bird.
top5.originality_score: 9/10. Nobody else will be doing pigeons, and the escrow is used as a clock instead of a payment. That moves it far from any generic shape.
top5.buildability_score: 8/10. The only fiddly part is crypto-condition encoding, so test it in hour one.
top5.biggest_risk: Ledger time is only accurate to 3-5 seconds, and a judge may ask why this needs an escrow instead of a memo. The answer: the commitment is public and fixed before release, so the secretary can't swap codes afterward.

top5.name: Naming Screen
top5.one_liner: Before a world-record attempt, you're given a random 5-letter name taken from the latest blockchain block and type it in as your character's name, which proves the run wasn't recorded beforehand.
top5.the_story: A speedrun moderator is looking at a world-record-pace run with a $5,000 bounty attached and has no way to tell whether it was pre-recorded. Naming Screen takes the latest XRPL ledger hash, turns it into a name the runner types on the game's naming screen, and anchors a hash of the run's splits on-ledger when the run ends. A verifier checks that the run fits inside that window, and two of three moderators co-sign the bounty payout.
top5.insider_detail: Runners pass a naming screen every attempt and normally type 'A' to save frames. Timing starts after naming, so a 5-letter name costs nothing. Bounties come in two kinds, 'first to beat X' and 'whoever holds it on date X', and time-locked escrows fit both.
top5.sponsor_use: XRPL ledger hashes are a public randomness source nobody can predict. A memo anchors the splits hash at the end of the run. Escrow with FinishAfter/CancelAfter handles both bounty types, and a 2-of-3 multisig matches how volunteer mod teams sign off.
top5.demo_moment: Left screen: Pokemon Red in an emulator, ledger #N gives 'QOMRA', and the runner types it in. Right screen: a 'faster' pre-recorded run is submitted, and the verifier turns red: 'this name came from a ledger that closed 14 minutes after your naming screen.' The honest run turns green and the mods co-sign the payout.
top5.real_vs_mocked: Real: name generation from the ledger, the end-of-run anchor, the escrows, the multisig and the timing-window verifier. Mocked: reading the name from the video (a mod confirms it by eye).
top5.originality_score: 9/10. Using a ledger hash as a freshness stamp that appears on screen inside the game itself is new. A default brainstorm stops at 'escrow the bounty'.
top5.buildability_score: 8/10. The build is simple. It's mostly verifier UI and a few XRPL transaction types.
top5.biggest_risk: It only proves when the run happened, not that it's free of cheats like splices or tools. Pitch it as stopping pre-recorded runs, not as general anti-cheat.

top5.name: Unblind & Pay
top5.one_liner: A lab that re-checks a published experiment gets paid at the exact moment its blinded samples are decoded, so nobody can see the result first and then decide whether to pay.
top5.the_story: A contract lab is replicating a hot mouse-tumor result for a biotech, using tubes labeled only A-F. If the result comes back null, payment mysteriously slows down. If someone sneaks a look at the code key early, the data gets quietly 'cleaned'. Here the funder locks the payment against a hash of the blinding key. The lab freezes its data on-ledger, and publishing the key both pays the lab and decodes the results.
top5.insider_detail: Well-run replications already have a neutral party, such as a core facility or an 'unblinded pharmacist', holding the key that maps tube codes to groups. That key is a secret that must be revealed exactly once, after the data is locked, which is exactly what an escrow preimage is.
top5.sponsor_use: An XRPL escrow with Condition = SHA256(blinding key) means the funder can't take the money back. A memo records the data hash as a 'data frozen' timestamp. Finishing the escrow with the key pays the lab and unblinds the data in one action. An optional Credential marks the key holder as an accredited custodian.
top5.demo_moment: The lab uploads tumor volumes for tubes A-F and the freeze hash lands on-ledger. The core facility clicks Reveal: the escrow finishes, the money lands, and the A-F bars recolor into Vehicle vs Drug, showing the result failed to replicate, and the lab still got paid. Changing one cell in the CSV afterward flags a hash mismatch in red.
top5.real_vs_mocked: Real: the conditional escrow, the freeze memo, the reveal, the decode and plot, and the tamper check. Mocked: the wet-lab data (a public replication dataset) and the core facility (a button).
top5.originality_score: 8/10. 'Blinding keys are already preimages' is a real insight, and paying regardless of the result is a sharp angle. It loses points because 'blockchain for science' is a known category, but this specific mechanism is new.
top5.buildability_score: 9/10. It's the smallest build in the list, which leaves plenty of time for polish.
top5.biggest_risk: It's less fun and less visual for a Most Creative track, and the people who'd use it next week are a small, slow-moving group.

top5.name: Ten Percent
top5.one_liner: Almond growers rent bees by the hive and currently get to choose which hives get inspected. Ten Percent hands that choice to the next blockchain block, waits for the contract's weather condition to actually be met, and pays the held-back rent by frame count.
top5.the_story: A beekeeper trucks 2,000 hives to a Fresno almond orchard. The grower's crew picks which 10% to open, finds weak hives, and cuts a $200k second payment. The beekeeper can't prove the sample was cherry-picked or that the inspection happened before the weather condition was met. Ten Percent commits the hive list on-ledger, lets a ledger hash choose the sample, and releases tiered escrows from a credentialed inspector's counts.
top5.insider_detail: UC Extension's standard contract says: 10% of colonies 'randomly as selected by the grower', no earlier than 14 days in, only after 4 straight days at 60F+ with no rain and light wind, inspected after 1 PM, against an 8-frame average with a 4-frame minimum. The two things that decide the money, who picks and when the weather clock starts, both sit with the party holding the payment.
top5.sponsor_use: XRPL: a memo commits the hive list, the ledger hash seeds the sample, tiered crypto-condition escrows pay by frame count, Credentials restrict scoring to a certified inspector, and Batch settles. Gemini's daily high-temperature markets (Sacramento) predict when the 4-day window opens so the 36-hour notice goes out automatically, and resolved markets confirm each qualifying day. Gemini is used for scheduling here, not hedging.
top5.demo_moment: The grower clicks 'Pick sample' and the app answers 'You don't pick. Ledger #N picks.' The Gemini panel shows the 60F+ days resolving, the ledger closes, and 40 of 400 hive dots light up identically on both parties' phones. The inspector enters counts, the average comes to 7.4 frames, and the 85% tier unlocks on the explorer.
top5.real_vs_mocked: Real: escrows, the ledger-seeded sample, Credentials, live Gemini temperature data and NWS wind/rain. Mocked: the orchard (a CSV of GPS points), the frame counts and the credential issuer.
top5.originality_score: 8/10. The insider sentence from the contract is excellent, and the use of the weather market is surprising. Some risk that judges hear 'agriculture + weather' and think insurance, so frame it as 'who rolls the dice'.
top5.buildability_score: 6/10. There are a lot of moving parts. Cut it to the sample draw plus the escrow tiers, with Gemini as a single panel.
top5.biggest_risk: Scope. And Gemini may only list Sacramento, and replaying 4 days of resolved markets might need captured data.

ranked.honorable_mentions: Slab Ladder: the most real-world option. It uses the live PSA cert API, and sub-flipping is something people do every day. It just lands closer to a 'conditional sale', so it's a backup if judges want practical over weird. Scale Rungs: the same escrow-ladder idea as Slab Ladder but more delightful, because the seed is literally named after the scale weight. Only build one of the two. Green Stamp: the line 'IRCs die December 31st' is gold, but there's a flaw. The QSO details can be guessed (callsigns are public and there are only a few time buckets), so the DX station could claim payments without the contact being in its log, which breaks the main promise. Lines-In: a strong idea, but it's basically Naming Screen set on a boat, so keep only one of the two. Upcharge Envelopes: a clever use of ERC-3009's 'sign now, settle later', but too much of it is mocked (invoices, price comps).
ranked.killed_as_generic: Melt Line: a weather trigger that releases money is parametric insurance with a cake on top. Fresh Questions: a gated marketplace with a refund. Strip the nouns and it's 'marketplace'. Strewn Field: a permissioned marketplace plus provenance, which is supply-chain provenance in costume. Window: a license token with an expiry date is the familiar 'licensing NFT', and it's too complex for 6 hours. Pencil: a production putting a deposit down to book a freelancer is freelancer escrow, even though the hold/challenge detail is lovely. The Open Jar: strip the nouns and it's 'provably fair raffle', a common hackathon project, and using a BTC market as a randomness source feels bolted on.
ranked.pick: Build Meta Lock. It passes the 'I've never seen that' test, it has the cleanest answer to 'why does this need a blockchain' (the answer is the key, so there's no answer server and no judge), and a 3-4 person team can finish it in 6 hours with nothing important faked. It also covers social proof, which the other ideas can't: run a real mini-hunt at the hackathon so other hackers solve the puzzles and claim a real testnet pot on camera, and end the video by opening an empty answer database.

obvious_ideas_discarded: Pigeon race prize-pool escrow / one-loft entry-fee escrow with refunds if the entry target isn't hit. This is freelancer-escrow in feathers and the first thing anyone would say.
Tokenized racing-pigeon pedigrees or result NFTs for auction buyers. It's supply-chain provenance for birds, which is banned territory, and it's the most obvious 'blockchain + livestock' pitch.
Heat-wave hedge for giant-pumpkin growers using Gemini's daily high-temperature markets. Pumpkins stall and split above ~90F, but this is parametric insurance with a new label.

A weigh-off weight-guessing market where the crowd bets on the pumpkin before it hits the scale. That's 'Polymarket for pumpkins'. The pigeon twin, an on-chain version of club 'sheet pools' and Calcutta auctions, is office pools plus illegal-betting baggage.
real_pain_points_found: Pigeon clocks are trusted, sealed hardware, and people have tried to cheat them. In 1950s Britain, fanciers believed mechanical clocks could be re-rated to read correctly when an official checked them, so clocks are set and physically sealed (welded seal) at the club before every race. Sources: https://www.ahsoc.org/blog/its-for-the-birds/ and https://heinzhistorycenter.emuseum.com/objects/52584/timer

Electronic timing systems (ETS) are a vendor gatekeeping fight. In 2022 the Belgian Competition Authority imposed interim measures on the Belgian pigeon federation for abusing its role in setting the ETS hardware standard. https://www.concurrences.com/en/bulletin/news-issues/september-2022/the-belgian-competition-authority-imposes-interim-measures-on-the-national

Race-result fraud is physical and clever. In Shanghai (2018), two men trained birds to have two homes, then moved them by bullet train hidden in milk cartons. Separately, chip-ring tampering gets raised as a cheating concern. https://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2018/08/cheating_in_bir.html and https://blog.vvsor.nl/2021/10/the-average-or-the-outlier/

Velocity is distance divided by (arrival minus liberation time), so everything depends on a trusted liberation timestamp, surveyed loft coordinates (great-circle distance, not road distance) and synced clocks. The liberation decision itself is made by a small committee, and in one documented case the race winner sat on the three-man liberation team. https://www.deduif.be/de/node/1545 and https://pedigrepro.duckdns.org/en/guides/how-to-calculate-pigeon-flight-distance

One-loft races take non-refundable perch fees, entrants give up ownership of their birds, and some prize pools are promised only if an entry target is hit ('providing we hit our target of 849 pigeons'). https://www.farmersweekly.co.za/animals/pigeons/one-day-loft-racing/ and https://marhaba.qa/katara-announces-one-loft-race-2026-with-usd205000-prize-pool/

In US club races, money changes hands in cash on shipping night through 'sheet pools' and Calcutta auctions (PETA estimated $54k at a single 2011 ARPU convention race). It's off-books, depends on trusting the secretary, and is legally grey. https://www.peta.org/features/pigeon-racing-investigation/explained/

Giant pumpkins get disqualified at the scale for a fingernail-sized crack or a soft spot reaching the cavity. A 2,520 lb Wisconsin fruit worth about $22,680 at $9/lb was DQ'd, and the heaviest pumpkin at Port Elgin 2026 didn't win because of a soft spot. Weighing on a tarp or pallet makes the weight unofficial. https://www.10news.com/lifestyle/wisconsin-man-grows-2-500-pound-pumpkin-but-crack-will-keep-it-out-of-record-books and https://www.cp24.com/news/canada/2026/10/09/northern-ontario-growers-giant-pumpkin-is-the-heaviest-but-doesnt-win/

Seed value depends on the official scale weight. Elite seeds sell for $200-$500, sometimes $1,500, and a record seed went for over £1,171. Travis Gienger said buyers would pay a 'minimum $200 per seed'. Growers can only estimate weight before the weigh-off with OTT charts that run hundreds of pounds off on oddly shaped fruit. https://mynorthwest.com/3935444/skorheim-giant-world-record-pumpkin-seeds-sell-for-how-much/ , https://www.irishnews.com/business/businessnews/2016/03/07/news/pumpkin-seed-bought-for-1-250-as-horticulture-firm-aims-big-442240/ , https://w.bigpumpkins.com/msgboard/ViewThread.asp?b=3&p=4963

ideas.name: Countermark
ideas.one_liner: A pigeon race clock that nobody owns and nobody can tamper with: the bird proves it got home by carrying a secret code on its leg, and typing that code in is what stops the clock.
ideas.world: Competitive homing-pigeon racing (club races and one-loft races)
ideas.real_person: A club race secretary in a 30-member combine on Saturday evening. Two members dispute 2 seconds on a 300-mile race. One has an old mechanical clock and the other a chip-reader ETS. The secretary has to open sealed clocks, cross-check the secret rubber-ring numbers against the basketing sheet he kept in a drawer, and explain why his own bird won. Everyone quietly suspects him, and the federation's approved-ETS list is a vendor monopoly the Belgian antitrust regulator had to step into.
ideas.insider_detail: Traditional clocking is already a commit-reveal protocol. At basketing, each bird gets a numbered rubber 'countermark' race ring whose number is recorded secretly by the club, and the fancier doesn't know which number his bird got. When the bird lands, he pulls the rubber and drops it into the sealed clock thimble. At clock opening, the club checks the numbers. A preimage-SHA-256 crypto-condition escrow is the same idea: hash(countermark) is the commitment, the number on the bird's leg is the preimage, and only someone holding the returned bird can read it. Velocity is surveyed great-circle distance divided by (arrival minus liberation), so the two timestamps matter more than anything else.
ideas.mechanism: 1) Basketing night: the app generates a random countermark code per bird, prints it as a tiny folded/QR leg band, and the secretary seals the basket. For each bird, the club account creates a small XRPL escrow (e.g. 1 XRP or the bird's prize-eligibility stake) payable to the fancier, with Condition = hash(countermark) and CancelAfter = race close time. The commitment is now public and timestamped, so the secretary can't swap numbers later. 2) Liberation: the convoyer at the release point taps 'Liberate', which writes a memo tx with GPS and time to the ledger. That's the official start, signed by the convoyer's key (optionally a 2-of-3 multisig with the liberation committee). 3) Bird lands: the fancier scans or types the code from the leg band, and the app submits EscrowFinish with the fulfillment. The ledger close time is the clocking time. 4) The race engine reads every EscrowFinish, computes velocity per bird from loft coordinates (haversine, yards per minute), and ranks them live. Birds that never home leave escrows that auto-cancel and return after close, which doubles as an honest public lost-birds report. 5) Prizes go out in one atomic XRPL Batch to the top N velocities. 6) An ElevenLabs 'loft radio' voice reads arrivals aloud: 'GB-26-K-04411, Thompson loft, 1,412 yards per minute, provisional first.'
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL crypto-condition escrow is the clock. Finishing the escrow is the act of clocking, the ledger timestamp is the arrival time, and CancelAfter is the race close. A database can't do this because the problem is that the secretary and the clock vendor are the trusted parties. Here the commitment is public before liberation, the timestamp can't be backdated, and no proprietary ETS box is needed. Batch handles atomic prize payout, and optional multisig covers the liberation committee. ElevenLabs is a bonus for the loft-radio voice.
ideas.demo_moment: A teammate walks into frame holding a stuffed pigeon with a paper leg band and unfolds the code. As they type it, the leaderboard reorders live, the XRPL explorer shows the EscrowFinish landing, and the loft-radio voice announces the velocity. Then the clock passes race close, and the escrow for 'the bird the hawk got' visibly cancels back on the explorer.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: xrpl.js on testnet; EscrowCreate with PREIMAGE-SHA-256 conditions (five-bells-condition npm, or hand-rolled DER); EscrowFinish; the liberation memo tx; haversine velocity from real lat/long (a real release point such as Sacramento into several Bay Area 'lofts'); the leaderboard; Batch payout if devnet supports it, otherwise sequential payments; and ElevenLabs TTS. Simulated: about 20 bot birds finishing on a scripted time curve, plus one live 'bird'. Risks: (1) ledger close granularity is about 3-5s while real races are sometimes decided by under 1s, so admit this and show ties broken by the ledger's tx order within a ledger; (2) crypto-condition encoding is fiddly, so test it in hour 1; (3) it doesn't stop the Shanghai 'second home' cheat, so say that upfront.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default move is to bolt payments onto pigeon racing (prize escrow, entry fees, betting pools). This idea comes from noticing that the sport's 100-year-old rubber countermark ring is already a hash commitment, and that an XRPL crypto-condition escrow is a drop-in replacement for the sealed race clock. The money is almost incidental: the escrow exists to be finished, and the finish is the timestamp.

ideas.name: Scale Rungs
ideas.one_liner: Sell seeds from a giant pumpkin that's still on the vine, at a price that's settled later by what the official scale says, with automatic refunds if the pumpkin cracks and gets disqualified.
ideas.real_person: A grower in late August who has a monster on the vine. It tapes out at 2,300+ lb on the OTT chart, but the chart can be hundreds of pounds off on a long fruit. Growers who already know her lineage message her for seeds. She can't price them: a 2,500 lb official weight makes each seed worth $200+, a DQ for a hairline crack to the cavity makes them nearly worthless as 'unofficial', and the seed's name doesn't exist until the scale says it. Buyers don't want to prepay a stranger for a pumpkin that might split in the truck.
ideas.insider_detail: Atlantic Giant seeds are named after the mother pumpkin's official weight plus the grower's surname ('2624 Gienger', '2365 Wallace'), so the product's identity and price are created at the weigh-off scale. Only an official weigh at a GPC-sanctioned site counts. A fruit weighed on a tarp or pallet, or one with a crack or hole that reaches the cavity, gets no official weight, and its seeds lose most of their value. Before that moment, everyone is guessing from OTT tape measurements.
ideas.mechanism: 1) The grower lists the pumpkin with seed reservations as XRPL multi-purpose tokens (MPT): N seed slots, each tied to that fruit's ID. 2) The weighmaster's site key publishes a set of weight-bucket conditions for that pumpkin before the weigh-off: hash(secret_<2000), hash(secret_2000-2199), hash(secret_2200-2399), hash(secret_2400+), plus hash(secret_DQ). 3) A buyer reserving a seed creates a 'ladder' of token escrows (RLUSD or another issued stablecoin; XRPL now supports token escrow), one per rung, each with that rung's condition and price (e.g. $60 / $120 / $250 / $450), all with CancelAfter = end of weigh-off season. 4) Weigh-off day: the weighmaster enters the certified scale reading in the app, which reveals only the matching rung's preimage, or the DQ secret. 5) Anyone can submit EscrowFinish for the matching rung, which pays the grower and settles the MPT seed slot to the buyer, whose seed now carries its official name ('2417 Smith'). Every other rung, and every escrow on a DQ'd fruit, auto-returns to buyers at CancelAfter. 6) Optional: the weighmaster issues an on-ledger XRPL Credential 'Official weight: 2417 lb, site: Half Moon Bay' to the fruit's ID, so later resales of the seed can show it.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL crypto-condition token escrow is the price discovery mechanism. A ladder of conditional escrows where only the scale can unlock one rung is something Stripe can't express. Stripe would need the grower to be trusted to refund, and refunds after a DQ are exactly where this community gets burned. The weighmaster, who is already the trusted authority on weigh-off day, reveals one preimage and never touches the money. MPT gives each seed slot a scarce, transferable identity, and Credentials make the official weight portable. Gemini, Agora and x402 aren't needed and shouldn't be forced in.
ideas.demo_moment: Split screen: a bathroom scale under a real pumpkin from a grocery store, scaled up by a factor in the app for demo purposes, labeled honestly as such. The weighmaster taps 'Certify 2,417 lb', the 2,400+ rung goes green on the XRPL explorer while three buyers' other rungs show as refunding, and the seed slots rename themselves from 'Pending fruit #7' to '2417 Smith'. Then rewind with the same setup, the weighmaster taps 'DQ: crack to cavity', and every buyer's money visibly comes home.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: xrpl.js on devnet or testnet; condition generation per bucket; EscrowCreate x4 per buyer; the weighmaster reveal; EscrowFinish; cancellation after a short demo CancelAfter (e.g. 3 minutes); MPT issuance for seed slots; and optionally a Credential tx. Mocked: the certified scale (manual entry, or a bathroom scale x multiplier), GPC site identity, and 3 buyer wallets. Risks: (1) token escrow (XLS-85) may only be on devnet, so fall back to XRP-denominated escrows if amendment status blocks you, and check in hour 1; (2) locking 4x the funds per buyer is a real UX cost, so be upfront that rungs could be narrowed to 2-3; (3) the weighmaster has to agree to run the app, though they're already the single trusted party in today's system.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default pumpkin pitch is a heat-wave hedge or a weight-guessing market. This one depends on knowing that the seed's name and price are literally the official scale weight, that DQs for cracks to the cavity are common and devastating, and that a set of escrows where only one can ever unlock is a cleaner settlement tool than any oracle-plus-smart-contract setup. It isn't insurance, a marketplace or a prediction market. The pre-sale is settled by a physical weighing.

obvious_ideas_discarded: Grade-prediction market: bet on what grade a submitted card will get. This is 'Polymarket for X' and a tipster market in costume, so it's banned.

On-chain provenance or slab NFT registry for graded cards and vintage guitars, with a token per cert or per serial number. This is supply-chain provenance under another name, and every card-NFT startup has already built it.
Repair-shop deposit escrow: the synth tech gets paid when the owner confirms the fix. This is freelancer escrow with a synth on top.

Shipping-damage cover for vintage guitars sent in cold weather, paid out from Gemini temperature markets. This is parametric insurance, which is banned. The friction behind it is real, though; see the pain points.
real_pain_points_found: Cards sit at PSA for a long time while the market moves. Regular turnaround has been 40-50 business days. People do sell cards 'at PSA' before grades post, but the buyer carries all the grade risk, so offers come in at roughly the PSA 9 price and the seller gives up the upside of a 10 (forums.collectors.com sub-flip threads; pregradecards.com/blog/psa-pause-flippers-resellers-impact; elitefourum 'PSA $$$ translates to raw $$$').

Crack-and-resubmit corrupts the population report. PSA can't tell that the same 1st Ed Charizard was graded 6 times, and high-value cards get resubmitted dozens of times chasing a half-grade bump. Population counts how many times a card was graded, not how many copies exist (forums.collectors.com crack-and-resubmit threads; elitefourum 'Crack and Release or Leave Well Enough Alone').

Declared-value upcharges arrive weeks or months after you submit. PSA bills them only once the card is graded, applies them inconsistently, and won't return your cards until you pay. In group or bulk submissions the organizer collects up front and settles the 'final cost' after grading, so one member's surprise upcharge becomes the organizer's problem to chase (elitefourum.com/t/psa-upcharge/29286; sportscardclub.com 'PSA Bulk Submission Group - May 2025'; allvintagecards.com/psa-grading-costs).

Middlemen who submit cards on others' behalf vanish or fail. When Ludkins UK collapsed, PSA took legal possession of every card submitted through it (1 Jan 2023) and returned them to owners. A YouTube group-submission service reportedly ran off with its last, largest round (psacard.com/communication; elitefourum 'Just a reminder').

Vintage guitar value depends on original solder and pot codes. CTS pot date codes are only meaningful if the pots are original, and techs replace pot internals while keeping the original solder joints just to protect value (es-335.com 'solder whispering', 2026; eddiesguitars.com pot-code blog; truevintageguitar.com).

Nitro guitars shipped in winter get finish checking if the case is opened cold. Forum practice is to leave the box shut for up to 24 hours, and people argue over whether to ship at all in cold months (rig-talk.com 'Guitars shipped in winter, do you let them acclimate?'; umgf.com cold-weather shipping threads; 300guitars.com).

Juno-106 voice chips (80017A) fail as the resin coating degrades. Owners struggle to find techs who will swap them, and shops take non-refundable diagnostic deposits with 'backlogs vary' (synthtopia; sonicstate 2021 voice chip replacement; maindragmusic.com repair terms). I considered this but didn't use it: every fit I found reduced to freelancer escrow.

ideas.name: Slab Ladder
ideas.one_liner: Sell a trading card while it's still inside PSA's grading queue: the buyer agrees a price for each possible grade, the money is locked now, and when the grade posts the correct amount goes to the seller and the rest goes back to the buyer automatically.
ideas.real_person: A Pokemon flipper sent a raw Moonbreon (Umbreon VMAX alt art) to PSA 35 business days ago. She needs cash for a sealed-box deal this week. A buyer on a Discord will only pay the PSA 9 price, about $X, because he carries all the grade risk. She thinks it's a 10, worth about 3X, and is stuck choosing between selling the upside cheap or waiting another month.
ideas.insider_detail: Grades appear on psacard.com (and through PSA's free public cert-verification API at psacard.com/publicapi) before the slab ships, and cert numbers are only assigned at grading. So there is a window when the card is unsellable at a fair price: nobody knows the grade, but everybody knows exactly when it will be known. The 9-to-10 price gap is often 3-5x, which is why buyers anchor on the 9 price. This is a fair-pricing tool for the existing 'selling at PSA' practice, not a bet.
ideas.mechanism: 1) Seller lists the card with its PSA submission number and the card identity (year, set, number), and proposes a ladder, e.g. any grade = $120, a 9 adds $180, a 10 adds $550. 2) The app generates one secret per rung and posts only each secret's hash. 3) The buyer locks the full maximum ($850) as three stacked XRPL escrows to the seller. Each uses a PREIMAGE-SHA-256 crypto-condition for its rung, with CancelAfter set to the expected turnaround plus a buffer. 4) When grades post, the seller enters the new cert number. The oracle calls the PSA cert API, checks that subject, year, set and card number match the listing (so a different 10 can't be swapped in), and reveals the preimages only for the rungs the grade cleared. 5) EscrowFinish pays those rungs. The rest can't be finished and return to the buyer at CancelAfter. If PSA marks the card 'authentic altered' or never grades it, no rungs clear and everything refunds.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL conditional escrow is the whole product. The buyer can see their money sitting on-ledger and can only lose it to one specific, verifiable fact. Neither side trusts the other or a middleman holding cash for 50 days, and refunds of the uncleared rungs are guaranteed by CancelAfter, not by a promise. A database plus Stripe would mean someone holding a buyer's $850 for two months and deciding who gets what, which is the Ludkins-style custodian failure this community already lived through. Optional bonus: issue the price ladder as a Credential on the seller so repeat sub-flippers build a record of honest ladders. Gemini isn't used and doesn't need to be.
ideas.demo_moment: The split screen shows a card at 'Grading' status and three padlocked escrows on the XRPL testnet explorer ($120 / $180 / $550). The seller types the cert number, PSA's API returns 'GEM MT 10', two locks open live and pay out, the third shows 'returns to buyer'. Then rerun with a real cert that's a 9: one lock opens and two stay shut. Use real PSA certs, with no hard-coded grades.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: XRPL testnet escrows with crypto-conditions (xrpl.js plus the five-bells-condition or cryptoconditions lib to make the fulfillment), the PSA public cert API (free token, rate-limited; GemRate's API is the backup), and a small Node oracle that holds secrets and checks card identity. Mocked: physical slab delivery after payment, and the 'submission number' step, since PSA has no public submission API, so the demo starts from cert entry. Key risks: getting the PREIMAGE-SHA-256 condition/fulfillment encoding right (do this first, hour one), and CancelAfter on testnet needing short demo timeouts. Being honest: the oracle that holds the preimages is a trusted party. In the pitch, frame it as narrow and auditable, since it can only reveal what a public API says.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: My default for 'grading + chain' is a slab NFT, a provenance registry, or a market on what grade a card gets. This idea needs three pieces of insider knowledge. Grades post before slabs ship. Sub-flips already happen but get priced at the 9. And the 9-to-10 gap makes a stepped payout the natural contract. It's a price-discovery fix for one 50-day window, and it uses escrow conditions as a price ladder instead of a yes/no gate.

ideas.name: Upcharge Envelopes
ideas.one_liner: When you join a group PSA submission, you pre-sign a few sealed 'if my card comes back worth more, here's the extra fee' payments, so the organizer can settle surprise upcharges the day PSA bills them and nobody's cards get stuck.
ideas.real_person: A Discord member runs a monthly 100-card PSA bulk group so members can get bulk rates. A member declared his card at the $499 value tier. It grades a 10 and is now worth $1,800, so PSA adds a tier upcharge weeks later and holds the order until it's paid. The organizer has to front the money or chase someone who has gone quiet, and 99 other people ask him daily where their cards are.
ideas.insider_detail: PSA upcharges are bills you only find out about after grading, and enforcement is case by case. Graders don't see declared value, so the upcharge depends on what the card is worth after it's graded. PSA keeps the cards until the bill is paid. Group organizers already say they will settle each member's 'final cost' once it's known, which means the liability is unknowable at signup and gets collected months later. That's the exact use for signing a transfer now and settling it later.
ideas.mechanism: 1) At signup the member declares each card's value tier. The app works out the possible upcharge for each higher tier the card could land in, e.g. +$X if it lands in the $1,000 tier, +$Y for $1,500, +$Z for $2,500. 2) The member signs one ERC-3009 receiveWithAuthorization per possible upcharge in AUSD on Base. Each has its own random nonce and validBefore = expected return date + 30 days. It's gasless, so the member needs no ETH and moves no money now. 3) The signed authorizations stay sealed on the app server; the organizer can see they exist but not the signatures. 4) When grades post, the app reads each cert's grade through the PSA cert API and maps grade to value tier from a public price comp. The organizer attaches the line-item upcharge from the PSA invoice. If the two agree, the app releases exactly one authorization and the organizer settles it on-chain. 5) Every unused authorization simply expires at validBefore. If a member calls cancelAuthorization beforehand, that's visible on-chain and the app flags their cards to be held, which is the same leverage organizers rely on today but made automatic and visible.
ideas.sponsor_use: ERC-3009's sign-now, settle-later behavior is the key piece. It's a payment that exists but hasn't moved, sized to a liability that can't be known for months, with no custody and no prefunded escrow tying up members' cash. Stripe would need a saved card and a charge 3 months later (with chargebacks, and organizers are individuals, not merchants). A database IOU is what they have today and doesn't work. AUSD gives a dollar amount that matches PSA's dollar fees.
ideas.demo_moment: A fake 3-member group sub: three members sign upcharge envelopes in a wallet popup with zero gas. Fast-forward: the app pulls three real PSA certs, and one comes back a 10 that jumps a tier. The organizer clicks 'settle', exactly one envelope opens, AUSD moves on the Base Sepolia explorer, and the group status flips to 'all clear - PSA can ship'. The other envelopes are shown with countdowns to expiry.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: EIP-712 signing of ERC-3009 authorizations (viem), settlement on a Base Sepolia AUSD (or a test ERC-3009 token if AUSD testnet access is slow), and PSA cert API lookups. Mocked: the PSA invoice line-item upcharge, entered by the organizer, since PSA has no public invoice API, and the grade-to-tier value comp, using a static comp table per card in the demo, which is a weak point. Key risks: confirm AUSD on Base supports ERC-3009 receiveWithAuthorization on testnet before committing (check in hour one; otherwise deploy a reference ERC-3009 token and say so), and the fact that cancelAuthorization lets a member back out. Present that honestly: enforcement is visibility plus the card hold, not cryptographic force.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: My default reflex for x402/AUSD is 'pay-per-request for agents'. The more unusual use is the ERC-3009 detail that a signature can sit unused as a conditional, expiring IOU. Matching that to PSA upcharges only works if you know that upcharges are discretionary, billed after grading, block the whole group's return, and land on a volunteer organizer. None of that is visible from outside the hobby.

obvious_ideas_discarded: Speedrun bounty escrow where fans pool money and moderators release it to the new WR holder. This is crowdfunding with a smart contract bolted on, and it does nothing about the actual trust problem, which is whether the run was real.
Betting on whether a streamer gets a PB or WR tonight using prediction-market odds. It's just 'Polymarket for X' and gambling on livestreams, so it's banned territory.
Minting world records or puzzle-hunt solves as NFTs or collectible badges. It's pure decoration and the chain isn't load-bearing.

Pay-per-hint for puzzle hunts or escape rooms over x402. It's generic pay-per-request, and paying real money for hints breaks the culture: hunts give hints out as earned or timed tokens, they don't sell them.
A marketplace where escape-room designers sell puzzle designs to venues. This is a generic creator marketplace.
real_pain_points_found: Pre-recorded 'live' runs. In the Pokemon Red Any% Glitchless scandal (2023-24), a runner (Jadiwi) submitted a WR-pace run that was really pre-recorded. A moderator asked him to reset his emulator to prove he was live, he went silent, and the run was scrubbed. It had been eligible for a $5,000 'break the record' bounty plus $2,500 for whoever held the record on Feb 1, 2024. Today the only proof that a run is live is a moderator asking you to do something on camera. Source: https://automaton-media.com/en/news/20240115-25522/

Speedrun bounties are informal promises with odd timing terms: 'first to break WR' versus 'whoever holds WR on date X', posted as news posts and paid by an individual. Examples: speedrun.com/mgsr '$1100 Cumulative All Courses WR Bounties', where the run had to beat the WR at submission time, and Wallet of Satoshi's 0.21 BTC Mario bounty with a live frame countdown. Sources: https://www.speedrun.com/de-DE/mgsr/news/nx9944x9 , https://walletofsatoshi.com/mario-bounty

Verification is slow and unpaid. speedrun.com says verification can take up to 3 weeks. Moderators of one game say it gets 40-50 submissions a day, and some runs sit for months while verifiers are away, so a bounty can't be paid until a volunteer gets to it. Sources: speedrun.com SMW/SMO/Minecraft forums, e.g. https://www.speedrun.com/de-DE/smw/forums/f7cr2

In randomizer tournaments (ALTTPR, OoTR), async qualifiers run on strict clocks: start within 10 minutes of receiving the seed, submit within 5 minutes of finishing, and getting a seed without submitting a time counts as a forfeit. Proving when a run actually started is all on the honor system plus a VOD. Sources: https://hthdev.zeldaspeedruns.com/event/s/8 , racetime.gg/alttpr rules

Puzzle hunts run their own economies of earned hint currency. GPH 2019 had 'advicebergs' (hint tokens) and 'answerbergs' (auto-solve tokens) released on a schedule. Other hunts use shop currency, for example 100 for a hint and 500 for a free answer. Source: https://www.puzzles.wiki/wiki/Hint_Currency

Hunt answer checking is centralized and fragile. MIT Mystery Hunt errata pages show answers that looked wrong because of typos, and one fix was literally 'call us and tell us what you think the answer should be'. Archived hunts note that 'not all parts may work properly' once the hunt server is gone. Since 2009 the MIT Hunt runs a fixed length after the coin is found, so the finish moment and prize are run entirely by organizers. Sources: https://web.mit.edu/activities/puzzle/2001/errata.html , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Mystery_Hunt

ideas.name: Naming Screen
ideas.one_liner: Before a world-record attempt, the game hands you a random name pulled from the blockchain that nobody could have known in advance. You type it in as your character's name, which proves the run wasn't recorded earlier.
ideas.real_person: A Pokemon Red Any% Glitchless moderator in Dec 2023, looking at a WR-pace run with $5,000 attached. All they can do is DM the runner 'please reset your emulator on stream right now' and wait. The runner goes quiet, and the community argues for a week about whether a run whose bounty was due by Feb 1 was pre-recorded.
ideas.insider_detail: Most RPG and adventure runs start on a player-naming screen that runners already pass through every attempt. They normally type a one-letter name like 'A' because it saves frames, and leaderboards time the run from a fixed point after naming, so a 5-character name costs nothing toward the timed run. Bounties also come in two flavors with different timing ('first to break it' versus 'whoever holds it on date X'), and only a time-locked contract handles both honestly.
ideas.mechanism: 1) A bounty sponsor locks the pot on XRPL in two escrows that mirror real bounty terms: a 'first to beat X:XX' pot and a 'holder on Feb 1' pot that can't be finished until FinishAfter = Feb 1. 2) The runner clicks 'start attempt'. The app reads the latest validated XRPL ledger hash and turns it into a 5-letter name in the game's own character set (e.g. 'QOMRA'), recording the ledger index and close time. 3) The runner types that name on the naming screen, so it appears on screen throughout the run. 4) When the runner finishes, the app hashes the splits file and the last 60s of the recording and posts that hash as an XRPL memo within a minute. 5) The verifier page then checks three things. The run can't have started before the ledger that produced the name. It can't have ended after the memo commit. And the window between them must be at least as long as the claimed time, so a pre-recorded or spliced run fails. 6) The game's moderators are a 2-of-3 XRPL multisig signer list; they co-sign EscrowFinish to release the pot to the runner, or let it expire at CancelAfter.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL is the core of this. Its ledger hashes are a public randomness source every 3-4 seconds that nobody can predict, including the organizer. The anchoring needs a source the runner doesn't control, which rules out a normal database: a database owned by the bounty host would just be trusting the host instead of the runner. Time-locked escrow (FinishAfter/CancelAfter) matches the 'holder on date X' bounty terms exactly. Multisig matches how volunteer moderator teams actually sign off. Stripe can't express 'payable to whoever holds WR at midnight Feb 1, if 2 of 3 mods agree, else refund'. Optional bonus: an ElevenLabs voice reads the beacon name aloud at attempt start, so it's in the audio track too.
ideas.demo_moment: Split screen. On the left, a runner opens Pokemon Red in an emulator; the app shows ledger #N and the name 'QOMRA', which gets typed on the naming screen. On the right, a pre-recorded run of a 'faster' attempt is submitted, and the verifier lights up red: 'name QOMRA derives from a ledger that closed 14 minutes AFTER this video's naming screen; run predates its own proof.' The honest run turns green, two moderator wallets co-sign, and the testnet explorer shows the escrow paying out.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: deriving the beacon from the XRPL testnet ledger, the hash-commit memo, escrow create/finish/cancel with FinishAfter/CancelAfter, the multisig signer list, and a verifier page that checks the timing window. Mocked: no OCR of the name from video; a moderator confirms the on-screen name by eye, which is an honest simplification. The demo can use a short game or a homebrew ROM. Key risk: it proves the run happened inside a time window, not that it's free of splices or tools. Pitch it as killing the 'pre-recorded run' attack specifically, not as anti-cheat.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default move is 'escrow the bounty and pay the winner'. This idea instead attacks the actual fraud from the Pokemon Red scandal (a run that existed before the bounty claim) and uses a quirk of speedrun routes, the throwaway naming screen, as the place to carry the proof. A ledger hash used as an on-screen freshness stamp is something only someone who has watched runners type 'A' a thousand times would think of.

ideas.name: Meta Lock
ideas.one_liner: A puzzle hunt where the prize money is locked in a wallet whose key is the final puzzle's answer, so the first team to truly solve it can claim the prize themselves, with no judge and no server.
ideas.world: Puzzle hunts (MIT Mystery Hunt / Galactic-style online hunts)
ideas.real_person: A volunteer running a small online hunt (writing team of 6, about 300 teams). They store the answer table on one server that leaks to testsolvers and falls over at kickoff. Every errata they post means hand-adjudicating 'we called in, our answer looked wrong because of your typo' (a real MIT Hunt erratum). And once the hunt ends, they must stay awake to confirm and pay out the prize.
ideas.insider_detail: Hunts already run token economies: GPH 2019 had 'advicebergs' (hint tokens) and 'answerbergs' (auto-solve tokens), and other hunts use solve-earned currency with fixed prices (hint 100, free unlock 50, free answer 500). Hunt answers are also normalized to uppercase letters only, so 'Pickle-ball!' and 'PICKLEBALL' match. That makes the answer a clean deterministic seed. Since 2009 the MIT Hunt also keeps running after the coin is found, so 'first finisher' and 'everyone else keeps solving' have to coexist.
ideas.mechanism: 1) Before kickoff, organizers normalize each puzzle's answer, then derive an XRPL keypair as scrypt(ANSWER + kickoffSalt), where the salt is published only at kickoff so nobody can precompute keys. 2) The meta's answer-wallet holds the prize pot. Each regular puzzle's key holds nothing; it only signs. 3) The hunt site stores no answers at all, just one public address per puzzle. When a team types an answer, the browser derives the key locally and checks whether it matches the published address. That's the answer checker, and it still works in the archive forever. 4) When a team solves a puzzle, their browser signs 'team <their XRPL address> solved P' with the answer key. Because the claim is bound to the team, another team can't replay it, and signing never reveals the answer. 5) A small relay checks the signature and pays the team's hint currency, an MPT that works like advicebergs, which they spend at the hint desk. 6) Whoever solves the meta derives the pot wallet and sweeps it to their team account in one transaction. A signature reveals only the public key, so watching the ledger tells other teams nothing. The coin find is now a timestamped ledger event.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL is the core. A wallet whose key is the answer is the only way for the prize to pay itself out with no trusted judge, and the answer never touches a server. MPT stands in for the hint currency hunts already invent every year, with a hard supply cap per release window. A Credential ('SOLVED: META') issued to the winning team gives an on-ledger finish record the community can cite. A normal database would need a trusted answer table, which is exactly what leaks, and Stripe can't pay 'whoever knows this word'.
ideas.demo_moment: Four tiny puzzles on screen. A teammate types a wrong answer and nothing happens, with no network call; the checker is local math. They type 'PICKLEBALL' and the hint balance ticks up as MPT arrives. Then the meta: they type the final answer, and within 4 seconds the testnet explorer shows the prize pot leaving the 'answer wallet' for the team's wallet. Then the kicker: we open the hunt server's database and show it contains zero answers.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Very buildable with xrpl.js: Wallet.fromEntropy on scrypt output, the address-match checker, signature-verify relay, MPT issuance and payment, the pot sweep, and a Credential on the winner. Write 3-4 small real puzzles so the demo isn't fake. Key risk: brute force. Hunt answers are dictionary phrases, so a cheap KDF is attackable. Mitigate with salt revealed at kickoff, expensive scrypt parameters, and a modest pot, and say so plainly in the pitch. Second risk: anyone who leaks the meta answer leaks the money. That's arguably a feature, since hunts already treat spoiling as cheating.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The obvious crypto puzzle-hunt idea is 'pay for hints' or 'NFT for solvers'. This uses the answer itself as the key: the puzzle's output literally unlocks the money, which deletes the answer server, the payout judge and the archive-rot problem in one move. It's grounded in hunt quirks (normalized all-caps answers, salt-at-kickoff timing, aceberg-style token economies, coin-found-but-hunt-continues) that you only know from being on a hunt team.

obvious_ideas_discarded: Pollination parametric cover: pay the almond grower if bloom week is cold (bee flight below ~55-60F). Discarded because it is the insurance idea again, just with bees.

Hive-rental marketplace or broker replacement: tokenized hive pallets on a DEX matching growers with beekeepers. Discarded as a generic 'Uber for X' marketplace. Brokers mostly handle relationships, not price discovery.

Hive-theft provenance tracker: GPS/NFC tags on boxes logged on-chain. Discarded because it is supply-chain provenance under another name, and real thieves move frames into their own boxes anyway (Mendocino 2022 case), so box-level tracking misses it.

Storm footage marketplace with crypto micropayments, or 'pay chasers per livestream minute with x402'. Discarded as generic pay-per-content/tipping. Stations do not lack a payment rail; they lack a reason not to just take the clip.
Prediction market on whether a tornado happens on a chase day. Discarded as 'Polymarket for X', and Gemini lists no tornado markets anyway.
real_pain_points_found: Almond inspection contracts gate the inspection on weather. UC Cooperative Extension Fresno sample clause (Shannon Mueller, 'Colony Strength Evaluation', ucanr.edu/media/306471): 'Upon 36 hours notice, the beekeeper agrees to open and demonstrate the strength of 10% of the colonies randomly as selected by the grower. Inspection is to be made after the hives have been placed in the fields for no less than 14 days and there has been at least 4 consecutive days of 60 degree weather temperature, no rain and no winds over 10 mph... after 1 PM.' Strength is typically an 8-frame average with a 4-frame minimum.

The 'random' sample is picked by the grower, the party who saves money if the sample comes out weak. Same UCANR deck: 'If the hive is in the orchard, it is part of the population. If the beekeeper doesn't want it to be counted, it should be taken out', so deadouts drawn into the sample count against the beekeeper. Selection is the trust point and nothing makes it verifiable. (ucanr.edu/media/306471; almonds.org 'Hive inspections: why they matter')

Split payment with the holdback at the grower's discretion: often 50% on delivery and 50% on removal, and 'if the grower is dissatisfied with the strength... the last payment can be reduced'. Beekeepers collect the fees themselves even when a broker is involved, so if the grower doesn't pay, the beekeeper takes the loss. (SARE 'Pollination for hire', sare.org; WCNGG 'Time to think about pollination contracts')

Enforcement drives price: Goodrich and Goodhue found 89.2% of almond contracts carry minimum-strength clauses, and contracts enforced every year pay the highest fees while unenforced ones pay the lowest. Inspections cost about $1.50-2.00 per inspected hive. (ageconsearch.umn.edu GoodrichAAEA paper; beeculture.com 2018 Almond Pollination Market Outlook)

Facebook Rights Manager hands storm footage to whichever page is bigger: when two pages claim the same video, 'the page with the most followers has the option to confirm ownership regardless of actual ownership', and management transfers after 7 days. Chasers who posted first had news outlets listed as owners, one licensed clip had 44,000 matches, and hijackers then file takedowns against the chaser's own licensees. (torrentfreak.com, 'Extreme Weather Videographer Faces Copyright Infringement Hurricane')

Storm-footage licenses are short, tiered and impossible to police. Veteran chaser Dan Robinson's rates: b-roll $250-300 with a 30-day max; severe $350-600 with a 30-day max; premium tornado/hurricane $600-1,500+ with a 10-day max and 'no online copies'. Local stations often cap paid video at $150, brokers undercut, and the producer reply asking to use a clip 'on all platforms with credit to you' undercuts prices across the market. (stormtrack.org threads 30740 'younger generation of chasers being swindled' and 30803)

Market exclusivity is how stations actually buy chaser coverage: Gray stations KCRG and KWQC signed exclusive local coverage with the Iowa Storm Chasing Network (iowaweather.com). Global Weather Productions has filed 100+ copyright suits against Nexstar, TEGNA and others, so unlicensed use is common enough to support a litigation business. (rbr.com)

California hive logistics: BeeWhere requires beekeepers to report hive relocations within 72 hours, and applicators must give 48 hours' notice to registered hives within 1 mile before spraying bee-toxic products on bloom. Hive thieves are usually other beekeepers, working at night when bees are dormant and moving frames into their own boxes. (almonds.org BeeWhere; cbsnews.com Yuba City theft; ourvalleyvoice.com 2022)

ideas.name: Ten Percent
ideas.one_liner: Almond growers rent bees by the hive and get to pick which hives get inspected. Ten Percent hands that pick to the blockchain's next block, waits until the weather clause in the contract is actually met, and pays the held-back half of the rental automatically according to the frame counts.
ideas.world: Commercial beekeeping / California almond pollination contracts
ideas.real_person: A migratory beekeeper from North Dakota trucks 2,000 colonies to a Fresno County almond grower at about $200 a hive. In week three the grower's crew opens the 10% of boxes the grower chose, finds a few deadouts and some 5-frame colonies, and cuts the second $200k installment. The beekeeper can't prove the sample was cherry-picked and can't prove the inspection happened before the contract's '4 consecutive days at 60F' condition was met, when cold bees cluster and frames look empty.
ideas.insider_detail: The standard clause from UC Cooperative Extension reads: 36 hours notice, 10% of colonies 'randomly as selected by the grower', no earlier than 14 days after placement, only after 4 consecutive days at 60F or warmer with no rain and wind under 10 mph, inspection after 1 PM, scored against an 8-frame average with a 4-frame minimum. A frame counts when 75% of both sides are covered. Any hive standing in the orchard is part of the population, so a deadout that gets drawn counts. Both levers that decide the money (who picks, and whether the weather window was really met) sit with the party who keeps the holdback.
ideas.mechanism: 1) At drop-off the beekeeper logs every pallet/hive ID with its GPS spot and anchors a hash of that list in an XRPL memo, so nobody can add or remove hives from the population afterward. 2) The grower locks the second-half payment on XRPL testnet as several token escrows, one per payment tier (for example 8+ frames = 100%, 7 = 85%, 6 = 70%, below the 4-frame minimum = 0), each with its own crypto-condition and a CancelAfter date. 3) A watcher tracks the weather clause. It reads Gemini's daily high-temperature markets for the nearest listed city (Sacramento; check whether Fresno is listed): live odds forecast when 4 consecutive 60F+ days will land, so the 36-hour notice goes out automatically, and resolved markets confirm each qualifying day. NWS observations supply the rain and wind parts. 4) When the window opens, the hash of the first validated ledger after that moment seeds a deterministic shuffle of the committed hive list and picks exactly 10%. Grower and beekeeper can both recompute it. 5) A neutral inspector whose wallet holds an XRPL Credential ('certified colony strength inspector', issuer mocked as a county ag office) enters frame counts for the drawn hives only. The app refuses entries from wallets without the credential and refuses hives that weren't drawn. 6) The app computes the average and minimum against the contract tiers, then reveals the fulfillment preimages for the tiers that were earned and finishes those escrows to the beekeeper in one atomic Batch. Unearned tiers return to the grower after CancelAfter. Both sides get a receipt listing the ledger seed, the drawn hives and the scores.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL carries the core of the idea. (a) Ledger-hash randomness after a public commitment removes 'selected by the grower'. A normal database run by either party cannot do this, because whoever runs it can reroll the draw. (b) Crypto-condition token escrows with CancelAfter turn a holdback the grower can quietly reduce into tiers that pay out mechanically. (c) Credentials restrict who can submit scores to a certified inspector without either party running the allowlist. (d) Batch settles all earned tiers in one transaction. Gemini's daily high-temperature markets are an unexpected input: the contract already depends on daily highs, and the market's live probabilities answer the scheduling question nobody else answers ('when will the 36-hour notice need to go out?'). Resolved markets also give a neutral record of each qualifying day. Stripe has no escrow tiers, and a grower-run spreadsheet is the problem itself.
ideas.demo_moment: An orchard map with 400 hive dots. The grower clicks 'Pick inspection sample' and the button answers: 'You don't pick. Ledger #N picks', with a countdown to the window opening. The Gemini panel shows Sacramento at 61F, 63F and 64F resolved, today's 60F+ bucket at 87%, and the 36h notice is sent. The ledger closes, 40 dots light up, one is a deadout in the middle rows, and both phones show the same 40. The inspector enters counts, the average lands at 7.4 frames, the 85% tier unlocks, and the testnet explorer shows that escrow finishing while the other tiers stay locked.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: XRPL testnet escrows with crypto-conditions (xrpl.js plus five-bells-condition for PREIMAGE-SHA-256), token escrow if the testnet amendment is live (otherwise fall back to XRP escrow and say so), the ledger-hash seeded sample, Credential issue/accept/check, live Gemini public market data for the city high-temperature series, and NWS API wind/rain. Mocked: the orchard and hive list (seeded from a CSV of about 400 GPS points), the inspector's frame counts (typed in), and the credential issuer. The inspector app holds the escrow preimages, so be upfront that it is the oracle. The credential limits who it can be, but it is still a trusted role. Risks: Gemini may only list Sacramento, not Fresno, which works fine for a Sac Valley orchard; the 4-day clause needs historical resolved markets, so check how far back the public API exposes settled events, and replay a recorded week if needed. Batch may not be on testnet, in which case sequential EscrowFinish calls work. About 4 hours for a 3-person team, plus 2 for polish.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default with bees is pollination insurance or a hive marketplace. This one starts from one sentence of contract boilerplate in a UC extension deck ('10% of colonies randomly as selected by the grower... after 4 consecutive days of 60 degree weather') and treats the trust problem as who rolls the dice and when the clock starts, not as payment or risk. The weather market here is used as a scheduling input for a contract clause, not as a hedge.

ideas.name: Window
ideas.one_liner: A tornado clip's TV license becomes a token that sits in the station's wallet for exactly its 10-day window and then disappears, with one exclusive per TV market. When a big Facebook page claims to own the clip, anyone can check the ledger and see who is actually licensed.
ideas.world: Storm chasers / severe-weather stringers selling footage to TV stations
ideas.real_person: A chaser films a wedge tornado on a Tuesday in May. Within 20 minutes she has a dozen replies from producers asking to use it 'on all platforms with credit to you'. One OKC station pays $600 for a 10-day exclusive. By Friday a 3M-follower aggregator page has re-uploaded it, filed a Rights Manager claim, and 'confirmed ownership' because it is bigger. Seven days later it starts sending takedowns against her paying station's own post. She has no public way to show who is licensed and who is not.
ideas.insider_detail: Chaser licenses are short and tiered by drama: b-roll $250-300 with a 30-day max, severe $350-600 with a 30-day max, premium tornado/hurricane $600-1,500+ with a 10-day max and no online copies (Dan Robinson's published rates, StormTrack). Stations buy coverage by market exclusivity (Gray's KCRG and KWQC took exclusive local coverage from the Iowa Storm Chasing Network). On Facebook, when two pages claim the same video, the one with more followers wins after 7 days no matter who shot it. So what matters is which DMA, which window, and a public record of first capture that a bigger page can't overwrite.
ideas.mechanism: 1) Within minutes of upload, the chaser's app hashes the master file and mints an XRPL Multi-Purpose Token issuance for that clip. The metadata holds the clip hash, tier and license days, and the issuance is created with clawback and transfer-lock flags. The ledger close time is the first-capture timestamp. 2) For each Nielsen DMA it creates a single exclusive unit, and it also offers non-exclusive units. 3) Offers sit on a Permissioned DEX inside a Permissioned Domain whose rule requires an XRPL Credential 'licensed broadcast newsroom' (issuer mocked as a broker or press association). Aggregator pages and random accounts can't even see the book. 4) A station buys with RLUSD or a testnet USD IOU. If the DMA unit is gone, that market's exclusive is sold, and a neighboring DMA can still buy its own. 5) Optionally, the clean ProRes master sits behind an x402 endpoint that serves the file only to a wallet holding a live license token, and the producer's ERC-3009 authorization in AUSD lets a station sign during wall-to-wall coverage and settle later, which matches newsroom invoicing. 6) When the window ends, the app claws the token back. A public 'who is licensed right now' page reads the ledger. 7) With Context.dev website-change monitoring on licensee and aggregator pages, the app flags any page showing the clip without a live token and generates a dispute packet: clip hash, first-capture ledger time, current licensee list.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL MPT clawback plus transfer-lock makes the 10-day window enforceable as state anyone can read, not a line in an email. Permissioned Domain plus Permissioned DEX means only credentialed newsrooms can trade, and aggregators are kept out by the ledger rather than by the chaser's inbox. One exclusive unit per DMA reproduces how stations really buy. The reason it is not a database: the people who need to check it (Meta reviewers, rival stations, brokers, a copyright lawyer like Global Weather's) don't trust the chaser's own records, and the first-capture timestamp has to come from something the bigger page can't edit. x402/AUSD is optional for the master-file download and pay-later signing. Context.dev change monitoring is the enforcement watcher.
ideas.demo_moment: A tornado clip goes up. Three station dashboards (OKC, Tulsa, Wichita) show the offer while a fourth tab, 'Viral Weather Daily', shows 'no access: credential required'. OKC buys the exclusive and Tulsa's OKC-DMA button greys out while Tulsa buys its own market. The demo clock fast-forwards 10 days, the token vanishes from OKC's wallet in the explorer, and Context.dev flags OKC's page and the aggregator still hosting it. One click produces a dispute PDF with the ledger-timestamped hash from 47 seconds after the tornado touched down.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: MPT issuance with clawback and lock flags on devnet/testnet, Credential issue/accept, and Permissioned Domain creation. The Permissioned DEX needs its amendment, so confirm on devnet in hour 1; if it isn't there, gate a normal DEX offer through credential-checked authorized trust lines (MPT RequireAuth) and say so. Also real: clawback on a timer (cron), SHA-256 file hashing, and a Context.dev monitor on two test pages that you control. Mocked: DMA list (3 markets), broadcaster credential issuer, the clip (any public-domain tornado video), and the aggregator page (your own test page). x402 master download is a stretch goal. Risk: Permissioned DEX availability; DMA exclusivity implemented as max supply 1 per DMA-specific issuance is simple but means one issuance per DMA, which is fine for a demo of 3. About 5 hours.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default for creators is tipping or pay-per-view micropayments. This idea is about license expiry and territory, which only matter if you know that chaser deals run 10 or 30 days with no online copies, that stations buy by DMA exclusivity, and that Facebook gives ownership to the bigger page after 7 days. The token isn't the product being sold. It is the license, and it is designed to be taken back.

obvious_ideas_discarded: Launch-scrub insurance or a bet market on whether a Falcon 9 / Vandenberg launch goes on time. That's parametric insurance or 'Polymarket for launches' with a rocket picture on it, and both shapes are banned.
Eclipse cloud-cover hedge: pay out if totality is clouded over at your site. Same parametric-insurance shape, and Gemini has no cloud-cover market anyway.
Paying SatNOGS volunteer ground-station owners per satellite pass they decode (x402 per frame). That is just 'pay-per-API-call' with a satellite skin.
Verifying meteorite authenticity by putting it on chain with an NFT certificate per rock. This is supply-chain provenance under another name, and an NFT can't tell you whether the rock is real.
A ham-radio contest prize pool or DXpedition donation-transparency page. That's the charity/DAO/office-pool shape again.
real_pain_points_found: International Reply Coupons (IRCs) are being abolished. The Universal Postal Union voted in Sept 2025 to end them on 31 Dec 2026, which is about 11 weeks from today. For decades they were ham radio's standard way to pay a foreign station's return postage for a QSL card. Source: https://www.arnewsline.org/news-text/2025/12/25/universal-postal-congress-ends-use-of-ircs-in-2026

What replaces IRCs is 'green stamps', meaning US dollar bills stuffed into envelopes to DX stations, and that cash gets stolen. Postal theft is described as common, Russian post workers are said to open foreign letters and remove valuables, and one South African DXer writes that 'a lot of mail seems to be disappearing'. Hams use double envelopes with taped corners to hide the bills. Sources: https://www.qsl.net/rz1ak/mail.htm , https://zs6ez.org.za/qsl-stat.htm , https://uksmg.org/content/qsling.htm

Payment and confirmation are tied together, but nothing enforces it. DXpeditions typically release the LoTW confirmation only after you pay through their OQRS, so you pay first and hope. LoTW itself works by double-blind matching (same band, mode group, start times within ~30 min). A miscopied ('busted') call or a wrong time means 'not in log', and the money is already gone. Sources: https://forum.log4om.com/viewtopic.php?p=13652 , https://lotw.arrl.org/lotw-help/developer-query-qsos-qsls/ , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logbook_of_The_World

Pirate DX operations transmit under unissued callsigns (ARRL 2017: fake 5H3 calls, per Tanzania's regulator), and eQSL can't tell a listener report from a real QSO. Hunters can't easily tell who is legitimate. Sources: https://www.arrl.org/news/pirates-on-the-air , https://www.amateurradio.com/eqsl-fraud/

Meteorite ownership goes to the landowner in most US states and in Canada. Finds are split by private side deal, e.g. 50/50 by mass at Buzzard Coulee or 70/30 under the AllSky7 terms. A Swedish court ruled that public-access rights don't let a finder keep a meteorite taken without a clear landowner agreement. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorite_hunting , https://researchers.usask.ca/gordon-sarty/documents/fireball/buzzard3.html , https://www.allsky7.net/docs/terms_conditions_allsky7_MWG_v1.0_2021-11-28.pdf

Fresh-fall material is sold before it is classified, and fakes flood in during that gap. Mifflin went to $50-300/g right after the fall, and dealers sold misidentified material (Campo del Cielo sliced and sold as Deport). Classification takes months to years. Rules require a type specimen of 20 g or 20% of mass, whichever is less, to stay with the classifying institution. Sources: https://meteoritegallery.com/mifflin-l5/ , https://www.meteorite-times.com/the-classification-process/ , https://meteorites.esci.umn.edu/umin-collection/classification-info , https://www.cbsnews.com/colorado/news/controversy-brews-over-meteorites-sold-on-western-slope/

ideas.name: Green Stamp (the QSL that pays for itself only if you're in the log)
ideas.one_liner: When you talk to a rare foreign radio station, you pay for your confirmation card up front. The money only reaches the station if your contact really appears in its logbook, and the payment and the on-ledger confirmation card happen in the same instant.
ideas.world: Ham radio DXing (chasing confirmed contacts with rare countries for the DXCC award)
ideas.real_person: A Berkeley ham chasing DXCC works a DXpedition on a Pacific island at 0412Z on 20m FT8. Before now he would mail $3 in green stamps double-wrapped in carbon paper, or pay the OQRS and wait months. Half the time the cash is stolen in transit, or the card never comes because he miscopied the time by 40 minutes and he's 'not in log'. After 31 Dec 2026 he can't even buy an IRC.
ideas.insider_detail: QSL confirmations already work by double-blind matching: LoTW only confirms when both stations independently upload the same callsigns, band and mode group, with start times within about 30 minutes. 'Not in log' (NIL) and busted calls are everyday failures. The traditional micropayment rail, the IRC, dies on 31 Dec 2026 by UPU vote, and the cash replacement gets pulled out of envelopes by postal workers. DXpeditions already tie 'pay us' to 'we release your LoTW confirmation' through OQRS. Green Stamp turns that informal handshake into an enforced one.
ideas.mechanism: 1) After the contact, the hunter's app normalizes the QSO into a tuple: both callsigns, band, mode group, and UTC start time floored to a 30-minute bucket. 2) It hashes the tuple into a PREIMAGE-SHA-256 crypto-condition and creates an XRPL token/XRP escrow to the DX station's address with that Condition, plus CancelAfter set to 90 days. 3) The DX station uploads its log after the trip. The matcher hashes every log line the same way, and any line whose hash matches an open escrow's condition is a confirmed QSO. 4) For all matches the DX submits one atomic Batch. For each hunter it does EscrowFinish (with the tuple as fulfillment) plus CredentialCreate, where the Credential is the QSL: issuer = DX callsign account, subject = hunter, type = 'QSL', with URI data holding the band, mode and time. 5) A busted call or wrong time means no match, so the escrow expires and the hunter's money comes back automatically. That gives an automatic NIL refund, the stolen envelope is gone, and there's no IRC to buy. 6) Optional: an x402 endpoint on the DX's QSL-manager site where a hunter on Base pays in AUSD with a signed ERC-3009 authorization that the manager only settles after the match. That is the same 'signed now, settled only if you're in the log' idea on a second chain.
ideas.sponsor_use: Both XRPL primitives carry the design. A crypto-condition escrow is a payment that releases only if a specific data string is revealed, and the hunter's QSO tuple is exactly that string. A wrong time or busted call yields a different hash, and CancelAfter turns 'not in log' into an automatic refund. Credentials make the QSL card itself a verifiable attestation signed by the DX station's account, which is what LoTW does with certificates. Batch makes 'get paid' and 'issue the confirmation' atomic, so neither side can take the money without delivering the card, which is the exact trust gap in OQRS/green-stamp QSLing. With Stripe plus a database, the DX operator or a middleman holds the money and decides whether you're in the log. That's the trust problem we started with. The x402/ERC-3009 deferred-settlement leg is a bonus, not required.
ideas.demo_moment: Split screen. Three 'hunters' each lock $2 for a QSO with a mock DXpedition 'VK9XX'. One hunter typed the time 47 minutes off. The DX drags its ADIF log file into the app, and ONE Batch transaction lands on the explorer. Two escrows finish and two QSL Credentials appear in the hunters' wallets, rendered as classic QSL card art. The third hunter's card shows 'NOT IN LOG', and a countdown refunds the escrow. End on the line: 'IRCs die December 31st. This is what replaces them.'
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: XRPL testnet escrows with PREIMAGE-SHA-256 conditions (xrpl.js and five-bells-condition), CredentialCreate and CredentialAccept, Batch (check that the Batch amendment is live on the network you use, and fall back to devnet), ADIF parsing (a simple text format), the hashing/matching logic, and QSL-card rendering of Credentials. Mocked: the actual radio contacts (use a sample ADIF log with ~20 QSOs) and a short CancelAfter (2 minutes) so the refund shows on video. Key risks: (a) the 30-minute bucket boundary. A QSO near a bucket edge needs the hunter to lock two half-escrows (one per adjacent bucket) or a matcher that tries both. Explain this honestly. (b) Batch may not be enabled on testnet. Devnet fallback, or a sequential finish-plus-credential pair. (c) The preimage stops being secret once it's revealed, which is fine because funds can only ever go to the DX's address.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: It depends on knowing three things a generalist doesn't: that QSL confirmation is already a double-blind hash-like match, that hams still mail physical dollar bills that get stolen, and that the IRC is being abolished on 31 Dec 2026. A default model reaches for 'NFT QSL cards' or 'tip the DXpedition', and both miss that the real product is a refund on 'not in log'.

ideas.name: Strewn Field (landowner-signed meteorite finds that can't be sold until science says they're real)
ideas.one_liner: After a meteorite falls on farmland, the farmer signs digital search permits.
