Every rock found under a permit is logged with its weight and GPS location, and buyers can pre-order grams whose payment only releases once the official Meteoritical Bulletin publishes the meteorite as real.
ideas.real_person: A Michigan soybean farmer wakes up to 40 strangers walking his rows because NASA radar showed meteorites landing on his land overnight. By law in most states the rocks are his. He has no idea who found what or what it's worth, and he'll hear 'I found it on the road' later. Meanwhile a collector in Texas is offered '$200/g fresh fall' from a dealer and can't tell if it's this fall, an old Campo del Cielo slice, or a Mifflin-style fake.
ideas.insider_detail: Most US states and Canada give meteorites to the landowner, and finds are split by private side agreements (Buzzard Coulee was 50/50 by mass, AllSky7 is 70/30). A finder can't sell legitimately until the Meteoritical Society's Nomenclature Committee approves a name. That approval takes months to years, and the classifying lab must keep a type specimen of 20 g or 20% of total mass, whichever is less. That gap between fall and approval is when prices spike ($50-300/g for Mifflin) and when fakes and mislabeled material flood the market.
ideas.mechanism: 1) The landowner's account issues an XRPL Credential 'search-permit:<parcel-id>' to each hunter who signs the split terms (e.g. 50/50). 2) A Permissioned Domain is created per fall and accepts only those permit Credentials. 3) When a hunter finds a stone, the app mints an MPT lot for it, carrying mass, GPS, parcel and finder in metadata. The split is computed automatically: the type-specimen reservation (min(20 g, 20%)) is earmarked to the classifying institution's account, and the rest is divided landowner/finder per the permit terms. 4) Lots trade only on a Permissioned DEX inside that domain, so a stone without a landowner permit has nowhere to be listed. That turns 'I found it on the road' into a provenance gap. 5) Collectors pre-order grams with token escrows. 6) Context.dev website-change monitoring watches the Meteoritical Bulletin Database entry for the fall. When the status flips to 'Approved' with the official name, the oracle service reveals the escrow preimage. The preimage was committed at fall time as H(fall-name || 'Approved' || salt). A single Batch then finishes all pre-order escrows and delivers the MPT grams, with proceeds split to landowner and finder. If the stone is rejected as a 'meteorwrong', CancelAfter refunds everyone.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL Credentials and Permissioned Domains carry the core of this. The landowner's legal ownership becomes the permission to trade, which a normal marketplace can't enforce because anyone can list anything. MPT lots capture divisible grams from one stone, with the type-specimen split handled automatically. Condition escrow plus a Context.dev change monitor on the Meteoritical Bulletin turns 'science says it's real' into the event that releases payment. Stripe holds the money with the platform, which then decides authenticity and can't encode the landowner's legal claim.
ideas.demo_moment: A map of a mock strewn field (drawn as an ellipse from a radar-detected fall track), with three parcels and three permitted hunters. A hunter logs a 34 g stone, and the app auto-reserves 6.8 g as the type specimen (20% of 34 g, since that's less than 20 g) and splits the rest 50/50 with the landowner. A rival tries to list a rock with no permit and the DEX rejects it on screen. Then the presenter flips the mock MetBull page to 'Approved: Lakeport (L6)'. The Context.dev monitor fires, one Batch transaction lands, and the pre-order escrows release to finder, landowner and institution at once.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: Credentials, PermissionedDomainSet, MPT issuance and transfer, condition escrows, the split math, and a Context.dev monitor pointed at a page the team controls (a mirror of a real MetBull entry) so the demo can flip it live. Mocked: the radar fall ellipse (static GeoJSON), hunter GPS, and the real MetBull page (don't wait months for an approval). Key risks: the Permissioned DEX amendment may only be on devnet and needs early verification, with a fallback of gating listings through domain membership in app logic and saying so. Also, the trust model hinges on the oracle service holding the preimage and revealing it on the MetBull change. Present that honestly as a single trusted watcher that could later become a multisig of curators.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default 'meteorite + blockchain' idea is an authenticity NFT. That fails, because a token can't make a rock real. This idea instead uses three quirks a generalist wouldn't know: landowners legally own falls, a 20 g/20% type specimen must be carved off, and the Meteoritical Bulletin approval is the real 'is it real' event that gates price. Market access hangs on the first and payment release hangs on the last.

obvious_ideas_discarded: Weather-day payouts for film shoots or outdoor weddings that pay out when it rains. That is parametric insurance, which is banned, and Sensible Weather + TCP already launched exactly this for film shoots in July 2026.
Same-day escrowed pay for background actors, released when the 1st AD checks them in. It is freelancer escrow and gig payroll with a film skin on it.
A marketplace for wedding vendor deposits with escrowed refunds. That is generic consumer escrow, and every hackathon has one.
A prediction market on whether a wedding gets rained out. It is 'Polymarket for X' and gives nobody a reason to use it.
real_pain_points_found: Film and commercial crews run on a 'hold' (pencil) system that is honor-based. A first hold means the freelancer promises not to take other work on those days, and the studio pays nothing for it. If a second production wants the days, the freelancer 'challenges' the first holder, who has about 24 hours to book or release. Nothing enforces the clock, so stale holds sit there and freelancers lose paid work. Source: Motionographer, 'Hold me, I'm scared: your guide to navigating the hold system' (https://motionographer.com/2019/03/11/hold-me-im-scared-your-guide-to-navigating-the-hold-system).

Short commercial engagements add an unpaid 'weather hold', a pencil for a contingency day that 'is not a confirmed day'. Crew carry this unpaid option on their calendars on top of the normal holds. Source: Screen Guild NZ, 'Weather Hold' (https://www.screenguild.co.nz/news/articles/weather-hold).

SAG-AFTRA 'weather permitting' calls: if the call is properly booked and the day is cancelled, the performer gets a half session fee instead of a full cancellation fee. 'Properly booked' means the specific day must be flagged as the weather day, not a multi-day range, which leaves room for disputes over what was flagged and when. Source: SAG-AFTRA 'Tips and Tools: Weather Permitting' (https://sagaftra.org/sites/default/files/tips_and_tools_-_weather_permitting_0_0.pdf).

Permit offices give one free rain date per booked date (Portland) or handle rain dates case by case (West Hollywood), so the backup day is on the location permit, separate from crew and talent availability. Sources: https://www.portland.gov/parks/film-video-and-photography-permit and https://www.weho.org/home/showpublisheddocument/17892/636511963555000000.

Wedding bakers and couples argue about melted buttercream. Bakers write 'not responsible for outdoor display' clauses and ask clients to sign heat waivers after warning them, and butter-based buttercream is much more heat-fragile than shortening-based or fondant. Melted-cake refunds still happen. Sources: Cake Central 'Buttercream And Heat' (https://www.cakecentral.com/forum/t/635629/buttercream-and-heat), baking-forums.com 'Outdoor wedding cake issue' (https://www.baking-forums.com/threads/outdoor-wedding-cake-issue.4250), mustsharenews melted-cake refund (https://mustsharenews.com/melted-wedding-cake/).

Florist contracts use 'equivalent substitution' clauses, and 'wilted flowers' is a recognized dispute type in demand letters. In heat, florists switch to hardy natives or silk where guests won't touch them, but someone has to decide before the stems are ordered, and that is days before the real temperature is known. Sources: terms.law florist demand letters (https://terms.law/Demand-Letters/Consumer/florist-event-decorator-breach-demand-letters.html), Easy Weddings '40 degrees flowers' (https://www.easyweddings.com.au/WeddingFlowers/advice/40-degrees-flowers/).

ideas.name: Pencil
ideas.one_liner: The film-crew practice of 'putting someone on hold' becomes a real queue with a real 24-hour countdown, so a production that sits on a hold loses the booking automatically.
ideas.world: Freelance film and commercial crew (DPs, gaffers, camera assistants, location managers): the first-hold, second-hold and challenge system, including the unpaid 'weather hold' contingency day.
ideas.real_person: Maya is a freelance 1st AC who owns her own camera kit. Production A put a first hold on her for Tuesday-Wednesday three weeks ago and has gone quiet. Production B offers a booked, paid Tuesday. She challenges A by text on Friday at 4pm. The producer is on a tech scout, nobody answers, and by Monday B has hired someone else. Under crew etiquette she can't drop A's hold unilaterally without hurting her reputation, so the stale hold costs her a day rate.
ideas.insider_detail: In the hold system the first holder pays nothing, and the challenge gives them about 24 hours to book or release. Etiquette is the only enforcement, so the deadline slips by default. Commercial shoots stack a 'weather hold' pencil on top that, in the Screen Guild's words, 'is not a confirmed day'. People outside production have never heard the words 'challenge' or 'second pencil'.
ideas.mechanism:
1) Productions and crew join a Permissioned Domain. Productions carry an XRPL Credential such as 'verified production company' from a crew-list admin, and crew carry ones like 'Local 600 member' or 'owns ALEXA kit'. Only credentialed productions can place holds.
2) Placing a hold writes a ranked entry (1st, 2nd or 3rd pencil) for that freelancer and date, using an MPT 'hold slot' per day or a memo-tagged tx, so the ladder is shared and timestamped.
3) Production B challenges by doing the thing that proves it is real: it creates a time-based XRPL Escrow paying Maya her day rate, with FinishAfter = now + 24h and CancelAfter a few minutes later. The escrow is the challenge clock.
4) Production A has two options. It can book by escrowing its own day rate within the window, in which case the app sees it, Maya doesn't finish B's escrow, and B's funds return when CancelAfter passes. Or it does nothing, Maya finishes B's escrow after 24h, and the ladder updates so B is booked and A's pencil is gone. Silence now has a cost.
5) Weather holds are a separate rung. For hot-weather exteriors (Phoenix, Sacramento), the weather-hold pencil auto-releases when the Gemini daily-high market for that city puts the shoot-day heat bucket below the production's stated cancel threshold. Maya gets the day back early instead of finding out the night before.
6) Optionally, ElevenLabs places a voice call to the first holder: 'Production B has challenged your hold on Maya Chen for Tuesday. You have 23 hours.'
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL is what makes this work. A time-based escrow is exactly a challenge: a funded offer that becomes binding when a clock runs out unless someone else acts. Credentials plus a Permissioned Domain fit a closed, reputation-driven community where you have to keep fake productions from spamming holds onto crew calendars. A normal database could store the ladder, but it can't make the challenger's money binding without a trusted intermediary, and the industry has no such intermediary today. Gemini's daily-high market only adds weather-hold auto-release for heat-sensitive shoots, and it's optional.
ideas.demo_moment: Split screen with two producer laptops and Maya's phone calendar. Production B taps 'Challenge' and a 24-hour countdown starts, compressed to 60 seconds for the demo. It is backed by a live testnet escrow you can open in the explorer. Production A's phone rings with an ElevenLabs voice warning. A does nothing, the clock hits zero, Maya taps Finish, and her Tuesday changes from grey '2nd pencil' to green 'BOOKED - B', with the escrow tx hash under it. Then a quick second run: A books in time, B's escrow refunds itself, and nobody had to send an awkward text.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: XRPL testnet escrows (EscrowCreate, Finish and Cancel with FinishAfter/CancelAfter via xrpl.js), Credentials and a Permissioned Domain created by a seeded admin, and a ladder UI from a few testnet accounts. Mocked: crew and production profiles, and a 60-second clock instead of 24 hours (an honest demo setting). Gemini weather-hold release is a stretch goal with a single read of the public market endpoint. Key risk: XRPL escrow granularity. FinishAfter/CancelAfter are ledger close times, accurate to a few seconds, so a 60-second demo clock is fine. Check the Credentials and Permissioned Domain amendments on testnet first, and fall back to devnet if needed.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: It isn't about paying anyone for work. It turns an unwritten etiquette protocol, pencils and challenges, into an enforced one, and you only know that protocol exists if you've worked in production. The default move is 'escrow the freelancer's pay'. The useful move here is to use escrow as a countdown clock on an option nobody pays for.

ideas.name: Melt Line
ideas.one_liner: Your wedding cake and flowers switch to a heat-proof version automatically if the betting odds on a hot day cross a line you set months earlier, so nobody argues afterward about who should have seen the heat coming.
ideas.world: Outdoor wedding vendors whose product physically fails in heat: cake bakers (butter buttercream versus fondant or ganache) and florists (hydrangeas and garden roses versus heat-hardy natives).
ideas.real_person: Dana bakes wedding cakes in Sacramento. She's booked for an August vineyard reception with a four-tier Swiss meringue buttercream cake, displayed outdoors. On Wednesday she has to decide whether to build in ganache and fondant, which costs $280 more and needs the couple's OK. The couple say 'it'll be fine'. Saturday hits 104°F, the cake slumps, the couple post photos, and Dana spends a month fighting a refund demand using a waiver they never signed.
ideas.insider_detail: The fight is about who chose, and when, given what was known at the time. The weather itself is not the issue. Bakers already rely on 'I warned you' waivers, and florists already have 'equivalent substitution' clauses. Both have a hard production deadline days before the event: the stem order or the cake build. Gemini lists daily high-temperature markets for Sacramento, SF, Phoenix and others in 2°F buckets, and they resolve against an official NWS station. That gives you a public, neutral, priced 'how likely is it to be hot' number at the exact moment the vendor has to commit.
ideas.mechanism:
1) At booking, couple and vendor pick a 'melt line', for example 'if the market says 40%+ chance the high is 92°F or above, go heat-safe', plus the upgrade price ($280). The couple put the upgrade amount in an XRPL crypto-condition escrow to the vendor. A CancelAfter just after the decision deadline refunds it if nothing happens.
2) At the vendor's real decision deadline (T-72h for the cake build, T-96h for the stem order), a small oracle service reads the live Gemini order book for that city and date and sums the implied probability of every bucket at or above the line. It writes that number on-ledger as an XRPL Price Oracle entry (OracleSet), so there is a permanent public record of what the odds were at decision time.
3) If the probability is over the melt line, the service reveals the escrow preimage, the vendor finishes the escrow and gets paid for the upgrade, and the order flips to the heat-safe recipe. The cake card changes from 'Swiss meringue buttercream' to 'ganache + fondant'. For a florist, hydrangeas become protea and kangaroo paw.
4) If it's under the line, the escrow refunds and the original design ships. The on-ledger oracle record is now the signed waiver: both sides agreed in advance that this probability meant 'not hot enough to switch'.
5) After the wedding, the same Gemini market resolves to the actual NWS high. The app shows the decision record next to the outcome, which ends the 'you should have known' argument either way.
ideas.sponsor_use: Gemini Prediction Markets matter here as a live, priced probability tied to a specific city, date and official station, available at a moment chosen by the vendor's production schedule. A weather app's '30% chance' doesn't settle bets and can't be audited later. XRPL crypto-condition escrow holds the couple's conditional upgrade money and releases it on a fact (odds above the line at time T), and XRPL Price Oracles turn the odds snapshot into a tamper-proof decision record. With Stripe you'd charge the couple once you already know it's hot, which is the conversation vendors are trying to avoid.
ideas.demo_moment: A cake-order card for 'Aug 16, Sacramento, outdoor, 4-tier SMBC' with a melt-line slider at 92°F / 40%. Hit 'Run decision deadline': the app pulls the live Gemini Sacramento high-temp book, shows the buckets stacking up to 47%, publishes the OracleSet tx, reveals the preimage, and the escrow finishes. The cake render switches from soft buttercream rosettes to sharp fondant with a stamped 'heat-safe build' badge. Run the same flow on a cooler SF date: 12%, escrow refunds, original cake ships, and a permanent receipt reads 'Both parties agreed: 12% < 40% at T-72h'.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: live Gemini public market data for daily-high markets (read-only, no trading needed), XRPL testnet crypto-condition escrow (PREIMAGE-SHA-256 via the five-bells-condition lib), and an XRPL OracleSet tx. Mocked: vendor and couple accounts, design renders (two static images per vendor), and the clock (a 'run deadline now' button). Key risks: (a) Gemini daily-high markets exist only for near-term dates, so the demo has to use a date within the listed window or replay a captured order book, and you should say so on screen; (b) the oracle service holds the preimage, so it's a trusted party, and you should name that honestly as 'a neutral bot that only acts on public market prices'; (c) watch that judges don't read it as parametric insurance. Frame and design it as a conditional purchase order with no loss, claim or payout, because the money buys a different cake.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default 'weather plus wedding' idea is a rain payout, which is insurance. This one uses a prediction market to make a decision before the event, not to pay after it, and it uses temperature, which nobody thinks matters at weddings, rather than rain. It rests on cake-decorator knowledge: butter buttercream slumps in heat while ganache and fondant hold. Florists have the same problem with hydrangeas versus proteas, and the decision deadline is set by the build or stem-order schedule. The escrow buys a different physical product.

obvious_ideas_discarded: Charter 'weather-out' deposit refunds that pay automatically off NOAA wind data or a Gemini temperature market. This is parametric insurance in a boat costume.
A prediction market or pre-bought calcutta on which boat wins a billfish tournament. This is 'Polymarket for fishing' plus an office pool.
A resale or transfer marketplace for Western States bibs and Wave permits, with XRPL tokens as permits. Both are explicitly non-transferable, so this is ticketing and scalping with extra steps.
Bot-proof permit lotteries where a 'proof of human' credential gates Recreation.gov. Generic, and the BLM's 2.1M-acre geofence already does a cruder version.
Boat-to-dock seafood provenance (catch to restaurant on a ledger). This is supply-chain provenance, which is banned and boring.
real_pain_points_found: 2016 White Marlin Open (Ocean City, MD): the winning boat's $2.8M was withheld because the crew failed polygraphs about WHEN lines went in the water. The case went to federal court, and the boat's electronics were used to show lines went in early. Tournaments rely on polygraphers and courts to establish a timeline after the fact. Sources: https://www.foxnews.com/us/the-one-that-got-away-not-the-fish-but-the-2-8m-prize.amp and https://courthousenews.com/judge-blocks-fishing-tournament-winner-prize-money/

Billfish release tournaments score fish that are never brought to the dock. Proof is the team's OWN camera footage. It must show the species, leader contact, that day's designated release card, and a time/date stamp that matches the official time from Tournament Control. Teams must not delete any footage, and they carry the camera to a verification site every evening. The 'release card' is a paper anti-replay token. Source: 2026 Sea Horse rules https://www.marlinmag.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-Sea-Horse-Rules_8.11.26.pdf ; Scrub Island rules https://www.marlinmag.com/tournaments/scrub-island-billfish-series/rules/

Releases are reported by VHF radio, and Tournament Control 'provides an official release time'. The timeline rests on radio logs plus trust. Source: Bisbee Costa Rica billfish scorecard https://cdn.bisbees.com/Content/Documents/Shared/BisbeeCostaRica_BillfishScorecard.pdf ; Big Rock blue marlin points require 'indisputable video or photo evidence' https://thebigrock.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/2026-Release-Form-FRONT-BACK.pdf

Hardrock 100 lottery: names were historically pulled from a jar at a board member's house, closed to the public. Forum posters said, in a board member's words, 'We think you're lying and you just let in all your friends'. An attorney alleged the lottery violates state and federal law, and the board responded by inviting human 'observers' to vouch for the draw. The RD also hand-picks about 6 entrants ('Dale's Picks'). Sources: https://ultrarunning.com/featured/hardrock-100-invites-observers-to-2017-lottery/ ; https://www.trailrunnermag.com/people/news/hardrock-lottery-lawsuit-controversy/ ; https://www.irunfar.com/2026-hardrock-100-lottery-results

Hardrock's service requirement: 8 hours of aid-station or trail work, proven by a paper 'Service Requirement Certification Form' signed by an RD or land-agency rep. Miss the form deadline and you are removed from the start list. Trail-work weekends also earn bonus and perpetual lottery tickets, which staff verify by checking 'archives' by hand. Source: https://www.hardrock100.com/hardrock-volunteers.php

Western States tickets double every year you lose (2^(n-1)). Applicants get about 270 lottery spots for 4,000+ entrants, so a single disputed ticket count is worth years of someone's life. Withdrawing forfeits your ticket history. Sources: https://www.irunfar.com/reflections-on-the-western-states-100-lottery-system ; https://dasz.substack.com/p/how-the-western-states-100-lottery ; https://irunfar.com/changing-times-at-the-western-states-100

The Wave (Coyote Buttes North): about 200k applicants a year for 48 daily slots. The daily lottery is geofenced to phones only, and permits are non-transferable except to the group listed at application. Lottery integrity is a constant theme. Sources: https://www.blm.gov/press-release/blm-kane-co-resume-wave-lottery ; https://kqed.org/news/11450483/cant-get-that-camping-spot-it-could-be-bots

ideas.name: Lines-In
ideas.one_liner: A billfish tournament timestamp that proves a release video was filmed after the official start and before the official stop, so nobody needs a polygraph to ask 'when did your lines go in?'
ideas.world: Offshore billfish release tournaments (White Marlin Open, Big Rock, Bisbee's, Sea Horse) and the charter captains who fish them
ideas.real_person: A Tournament Control volunteer at the Big Rock weigh station at 6pm. Forty boats are lined up with GoPros. A protest has been filed claiming a boat's 'first blue release' clip was shot before the 7:30 lines-in. All she has is a camera clock the team set themselves, a paper release card, and a VHF log, and $500k of calcutta money depends on her call. The alternative is what White Marlin Open did in 2016: polygraph everyone and go to federal court.
ideas.insider_detail: Release tournaments already run a crude commit-reveal scheme. Every day there is a 'designated release card' that must appear in the video so a team can't reuse old footage, and Tournament Control 'provides the official release time' over VHF. The paper card only proves the video wasn't shot before the card existed. It proves nothing about lines-out, and nothing about whether the footage was edited later. The $2.8M White Marlin Open case turned entirely on lines-in timing.
ideas.mechanism: 1) The night before, Tournament Control picks a secret word for tomorrow's release card and creates an XRPL crypto-condition escrow. The condition is the hash of that word, and the escrow holds the day's calcutta 'daily level' pot. The commitment is now public and can't be changed. 2) At lines-in, Control finishes the escrow by revealing the word. The reveal is on-ledger with a ledger close time, and an ElevenLabs voice reads it over the radio feed: 'Lines in, lines in, today's code is ALBACORE-7'. 3) When the mate releases a fish, the boat's phone app hashes the video file and submits an XRPL tx with memo {team, angler, species, sha256}. That gives the video a public timestamp about 4 seconds later, from whatever cell or Starlink signal the boat has. If there's no signal, the app signs the memo offline and the tx's LastLedgerSequence shows when it was actually submitted. 4) At the dock, a judge drops the video file into the verifier page. The page recomputes the hash, finds the on-ledger tx, and checks that tx time falls between the lines-in reveal and lines-out. A judge confirms the code is visible in the video. The verdict is 'filmed inside the bracket' or not. 5) Calcutta payouts for each level are XRPL token escrows that release when the protest window closes. A protest becomes a check against public timestamps.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL is essential twice over. (a) Crypto-condition escrow is the commit-reveal: the start-of-fishing secret is cryptographically committed the night before and revealed with a public timestamp, so Control can't 'leak' it early to a friend boat without it being provable. (b) Ledger close times are a neutral clock that neither the boat (which sets its own GoPro clock) nor the committee (which keeps the VHF log) controls. A normal database gives you a timestamp the committee could edit, which is exactly the trust problem in the Heasley case. ElevenLabs is a bonus for the authentic VHF announcement in the demo.
ideas.demo_moment: Split screen. Left: a radio crackle plays 'Lines in, today's code is MAHI-42' (ElevenLabs), and the escrow finish lands on the XRPL testnet explorer. Right: a teammate films a toy marlin with a card reading MAHI-42, and the app's tx lands 4 seconds later. Then a 'cheater' clip, filmed earlier with a guessed code, gets dropped into the verifier and flashes red: 'hash first seen 07:12, lines-in 07:30'. A third clip is re-encoded and trimmed, and the verifier shows 'no ledger anchor, this is not the original footage'.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: xrpl.js on testnet for EscrowCreate/EscrowFinish with a PREIMAGE-SHA-256 condition (five-bells-condition lib), memo txs, ledger-time lookup, in-browser SHA-256 of a video file, and an ElevenLabs TTS clip. Mocked: the boat's satellite uplink (just a phone on wifi), and the human check that the code word appears in the video (judge ticks a box, or run a quick OCR as a stretch). Key risk: crypto-condition encoding in xrpl.js is fiddly. Budget an hour, and fall back to a hash commit posted in a memo with the reveal in a later memo if needed. Second risk: judges may ask 'what if they hash a video they shot before lines-in?' The answer is that the code didn't exist yet, so the two halves together are the whole point and must both be in the demo.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default fishing ideas are about money (calcutta betting, charter deposits, weather refunds). This one comes from a rulebook clause about a daily paper card and a court case about lines-in timing. Its core is a time-window proof built from a commit-reveal escrow, not a payment, and it only makes sense if you know release tournaments score fish that never reach the dock.

ideas.name: The Open Jar
ideas.one_liner: A trail-race entry lottery that anyone can re-run at home to check the winners, where your volunteer hours count as tickets because the aid-station captain signed them on-ledger instead of on a paper form.
ideas.world: Lottery-entry ultramarathons: Hardrock 100, Western States 100, and the hundreds of smaller races that copy them
ideas.real_person: Hardrock's lottery coordinator in Silverton in December. Last time she pulled names from a jar in a board member's living room, the forums said 'you just let in all your friends', an attorney blogged that the lottery was illegal, and she now flies in 'independent observers' to vouch for her. Meanwhile she is matching about 2,700 applicants' claimed trail-work hours against scanned certification forms signed by RDs she has never met, and anyone who misses the form deadline gets cut from the start list.
ideas.insider_detail: Hardrock tickets depend on a mess of rules. Ticket counts come from finishes, years applied, perpetual tickets earned per five years of volunteering, one-time tickets for trail work on both days, a bonus for certified 'Trail Bosses', and a mandatory 8-hour service requirement proven by a signed paper form. Western States tickets double every losing year (2^(n-1)), so one miscounted year is a multi-year setback. The trust problem isn't only the draw. Nobody can see whether everyone else's ticket count is right.
ideas.mechanism: 1) Issuers: aid-station captains and trail-crew leaders hold an XRPL account that the race has accepted as a trusted issuer. After a shift, the captain issues an XRPL Credential (CredentialCreate, e.g. type 'HR-SERVICE-2027-8H' or 'TRAIL-BOSS') to the volunteer's account, and the volunteer accepts it. That replaces the paper form. 2) Gate: lottery entry is a Permissioned Domain. You can only submit an entry tx if you hold the required service credential, so the 'removed from the start list' check runs automatically. 3) Ticket math: a public script reads each entrant's credentials and their prior-years entry history on-ledger and computes tickets with the race's real formula. The full ticket list is published, and anyone can dispute their own row before close. 4) Commit: before entries close, the RD creates a crypto-condition escrow whose condition is H(secret). The RD also publishes RD picks ('Dale's Picks') as credentials, so they are on the record before the draw instead of after. 5) Beacon: the draw seed = SHA-256(RD secret, which the RD reveals by finishing the escrow, plus the official settlement of a pre-named Gemini hourly BTC up/down market at a pre-named hour, plus the frozen ticket-list hash). The RD can't predict the market, and the market doesn't know the RD's secret, so nobody controls the seed. 6) The draw is a deterministic weighted shuffle from that seed, and anyone can run it in the browser and get the same winners and waitlist order.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL Credentials replace the signed paper service form with an attestation from a named captain that anyone can check and that can be revoked. Permissioned Domains turn 'you must have done service to enter' into a rule enforced at the ledger. A crypto-condition escrow forces the RD to commit to their randomness before the draw and reveal it publicly. The Gemini Prediction Markets API is the unexpected input: an hourly crypto market's official resolution, with a named resolution source, works as a public randomness beacon nobody in trail running can influence. A Google Form plus a spreadsheet RNG is exactly what generated the 'you let in your friends' accusations, so a normal database is the problem here, not the fix.
ideas.demo_moment: The RD clicks 'Draw' at 4:00pm. The Gemini hourly BTC market for 3-4pm resolves, the escrow reveal lands, and the winners list animates out of a jar. Then a 'skeptical runner' on a second laptop opens the static verifier page, which has no server, pastes the ledger tx hashes, and gets the identical 146 names in the identical waitlist order. Then the RD tries to swap in a friend by editing one ticket count. The ticket-list hash no longer matches the one committed on-ledger, and the verifier turns red.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: XRPL Credentials (CredentialCreate/Accept) and Permissioned Domains on devnet/testnet via xrpl.js, escrow commit-reveal, the Gemini public market-data endpoint to fetch a real hourly BTC market's resolution, and a deterministic seeded weighted draw in JS (about 50 lines). Mocked: the applicants (a seeded set of about 300 fake runners with plausible histories) and the aid-station captain UI (a simple 'issue credential' button). Key risk: Permissioned Domain support in the xrpl.js version and network. If gating isn't ready, show the credential check client-side and say so. Also, the waiting hour for a real market to settle won't fit a 2-minute video, so point at an already-resolved market and show its timestamp.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The obvious race-lottery ideas are bib resale, bot blocking or 'NFT bibs'. This idea is about a verification job most people don't know exists: race staff checking a signed paper form for 8 hours of aid-station work, done in a town of 600 people. It uses a prediction market as a randomness beacon instead of something to bet on, and it starts from a specific scandal, the board-member's-living-room jar.

obvious_ideas_discarded: Preregistration timestamping: hash your hypothesis onto a chain before you run the study. This is the cliché DeSci pitch, and OSF already timestamps preregistrations for free.

Paid peer review or reviewer tokens, for example a $450-per-review payment rail or reputation points for reviewers. Heathers' #450movement already exists and the Critical Care Medicine and Biology Open trials have run, so this just puts a payment rail on a known debate.
A reagent or antibody marketplace with on-chain 'validation scores'. That is CiteAb or Antibodypedia plus a token, a generic marketplace for X.
A student note-sharing or used-textbook resale marketplace. It is the student-startup angle the brief bans, and Course Hero, OneClass and Notehall are already here.
Paying or bidding to jump the office-hours queue. It is ethically DOA (rich kids get help first) and it is a 'pay-per-request' shape.
real_pain_points_found: Paid replications can be pushed toward a particular result. In the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, 32% of experiments had original authors who were unhelpful or unresponsive, about 70% needed key reagents from the original authors, and only 50 of 193 planned experiments were finished. Whoever pays for a replication has a stake in how it turns out. Source: eLife 'Challenges for assessing replicability in preclinical cancer biology' https://elifesciences.org/articles/67995 and https://www.cos.io/rpcb

Error-hunting in science is now paid like bug bounties, but authors have to opt in. The ERROR project pays reviewers up to CHF 1,000 plus a bonus of up to CHF 2,500 depending on the size of the errors found, and pays authors CHF 250 to take part plus a bonus if few errors turn up. The payout depends on the result, so the money is outcome-contingent by design. Source: https://www.thetransmitter.org/publishing/bounty-hunting-for-blunders-qa-with-russell-poldrack-and-jan-wessel/ and https://academica.ca/top-ten/error-project-compensates-reviewers-who-spot-mistakes-in-published-papers-opinion/

Antibody lots drift. Less than half of research antibodies pass independent validation, and monoclonal hybridomas drift over decades of passaging while the old datasheet stays attached. Labs work around this by reserving a single 'good lot' from Cell Signaling or Proteintech for a whole project. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6930532 and https://cellsignal.com/services/bulk-quantities-and-lot-reservations

Unleaked exam questions are a scarce, perishable asset. A University of Oregon chemistry instructor said Chegg 'has every single question from every single test bank that I have ever seen.' At North Dakota State, Chegg experts answered exam questions posted mid-exam in about 30 minutes. Chegg's 'Honor Shield' lets professors pre-submit questions to block them during an exam window. Sources: https://dailyemerald.com/?p=79540 and https://workspaces.ndsu.edu/fileadmin/coe/College_Happenings_Archive/2021/College_Happenings_March_2__2021.pdf and https://cavalierdaily.com/article/2020/09/professors-seek-information-on-students-using-online-services-for-assignments

Instructors fall back on publisher test banks because writing original questions takes time. Those banks are the ones that leak, so adjuncts teaching the same intro course at many schools each rewrite exams alone, unpaid. Source: University of Oregon / Daily Emerald coverage above, and the TAMU report https://static.texastribune.org/media/files/4ecefc60488aab0aeabbcd681304075b/TAMU.pdf

Course staff overwork in office hours. Before deadlines, queues spike and tickets are capped at 5–15 minutes. Staff have to choose between 'volunteering extra time or abandoning students still on the queue,' and students give up after about 49 minutes. Sources: https://pedagogy.cs161.org/2022/01/14/notes-on-office-hour-queues/ and https://sigcse2024.sigcse.org/details/sigcse-ts-2024-posters/42/Using-Survival-Analysis-to-Model-Students-Patience-in-Online-Office-Hour-Queues-

Selling desk copies is an open secret. Roving independent book buyers go office to office buying 'Complimentary Copy, Not for Resale' textbooks from professors. Colleges such as Vol State write policies calling it unethical, and adjuncts often get no desk copies at all. Sources: https://pittnews.com/article/37951/archives/book-center-safeguards-cant-stop-all-complimentary-texts and https://volstate.edu/policies/ii0114-re-selling-examination-copies-textbooks-policy

ideas.name: Unblind & Pay
ideas.one_liner: A replication lab gets paid at the exact moment its blinded samples are decoded, so nobody can see the result first and then decide whether to pay or whether to tweak the data.
ideas.world: A: replication crisis (preclinical replications, ERROR-style audits, pharma checking academic targets before licensing)
ideas.real_person: A postdoc at a contract lab hired by a biotech to replicate a hot mouse-tumor result before the biotech licenses it. The lab receives tubes labeled only A–F, coded by a core facility. Its annoying moment: it delivers a null result and the client's renewal and payment suddenly slow down. Or, from the other side, someone peeks at the code key before the data is locked, and the result quietly gets 'cleaned'.
ideas.insider_detail: Good replications are blinded. A neutral party, such as a core facility or the 'unblinded pharmacist' in clinical-trial practice, holds the randomization key that maps tube codes to treatment groups. That key is already a secret string that must be revealed exactly once, after the data is frozen. That is exactly what a PREIMAGE-SHA-256 crypto-condition is. Registered Reports already make publication independent of outcome through 'in-principle acceptance'; nothing does the same for payment.
ideas.mechanism: 1) The core facility generates the blinding key (the tube-code to group mapping plus a salt) and gives only SHA256(key) to the funder. 2) The funder creates an XRPL escrow to the replication lab with Condition = that hash and a long CancelAfter. From then on the funder cannot claw the money back early. 3) The lab runs the blinded experiment and posts SHA256(raw data CSV) as a memo transaction, which is an on-ledger 'data frozen' timestamp. 4) A watcher sees the freeze memo, and the core publishes the key on-ledger. 5) Anyone, including the lab's bot, submits EscrowFinish with that key as fulfillment, and the payment lands. 6) The same key decodes the CSV in the app, and the effect-size plot renders: replicated or not. Payment and unblinding are the same act, so the money cannot depend on the outcome, and the data provably existed before anyone could decode it. Optional: an XRPL Credential identifies the core as an accredited 'blinding custodian', so funders can check who holds the key.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL conditional escrow carries the idea. The scientific secret, the unblinding key, becomes the payment fulfillment. A normal database or Stripe would need a trusted platform to hold the key and the money, which recreates the conflict of interest. Here the money is locked before results exist, nobody can redirect it, and it is released by publishing the key. Ledger memos give a neutral 'data frozen before unblinding' timestamp. Credentials are an optional bonus for the custodian role. Do not bolt on Gemini.
ideas.demo_moment: Split screen. The lab uploads a CSV of tumor volumes for tubes A–F, and a 'Data frozen' memo hash appears on the testnet explorer. The core clicks Reveal. In one beat the escrow flips to Finished, 500 XRP lands in the lab wallet, and the anonymous A–F bars recolor into Vehicle vs Drug and show the result failed to replicate. The lab got paid anyway. Then a 'peek attempt' shows that changing one cell in the CSV after freezing produces a hash mismatch, flagged red.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: XRPL testnet escrow with a PREIMAGE-SHA-256 condition (five-bit-condition or xrpl.js cryptoconditions helper), a memo for the data hash, EscrowFinish, a small web UI that decodes groups and plots them, and a hash-mismatch check. Mocked: the actual wet-lab data (use a published RPCB dataset or synthetic data) and the core facility (a button). Main risk: encoding the crypto-condition and fulfillment correctly. Budget an hour for it, since the DER encoding of condition and fulfillment is a common gotcha. Also, a conditional escrow needs a CancelAfter or FinishAfter set.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default blockchain-for-science pitch is 'timestamp your preregistration' or 'tokenize peer review.' This instead notices that blinding keys are already preimages, and it targets a narrower and nastier problem: payment that depends on the outcome, plus peeking before data is frozen. It takes a lab-practice detail (who holds the randomization key) and makes it the cryptographic object.

ideas.name: Fresh Questions
ideas.one_liner: Instructors who teach the same intro course at different schools can sell each other exam questions that have never been online, and a buyer gets a refund if a question turns out to be already leaked.
ideas.world: B: the course-materials economy from the instructor and adjunct side (Calc I, Gen Chem, Intro Stats, Intro Accounting taught by thousands of adjuncts)
ideas.real_person: An adjunct teaching three sections of Intro Stats at two community colleges for about $4k per course, with no paid time for writing exams. Their annoying moment: the night before the midterm they realize every publisher test-bank question is on Chegg already, so they rewrite 25 questions alone at 1am. Meanwhile another adjunct 40 miles away has a pile of good original questions sitting unused.
ideas.insider_detail: In this economy the scarce good is not textbooks or notes. It is how fresh a question is: whether it has never been online. Questions lose value the moment they appear on Chegg, Quizlet or Course Hero, sometimes within 30 minutes of an exam starting. The asset only keeps value if students can never get it, so the market has to be closed to non-instructors. Chegg's own 'Honor Shield' (pre-submitting questions to block answers during an exam window) shows the exam window is the unit that matters.
ideas.mechanism: 1) An instructor gets an XRPL Credential 'verified instructor of record' from a department-chair account, which acts as the issuer. 2) They list a question pack as an MPT with RequireAuth plus Clawback and Lock enabled. Only credentialed accounts can hold it, and the content is delivered encrypted off-chain to holders. 3) Buyers trade packs on a Permissioned DEX (or, as a fallback, an auth-gated direct payment) inside a Permissioned Domain that admits only instructor credentials. Students cannot even see the order book. 4) Payment goes to the seller through a conditional escrow that runs until the buyer's exam ends. 5) Context.dev website-change monitoring watches Chegg, Quizlet and Course Hero search for fingerprint phrases from each question. 6) If a question surfaces before the buyer's exam, the oracle withholds the preimage. The escrow then runs out to CancelAfter and refunds the buyer, the seller's remaining tokens of that pack are locked or clawed back, and the leak count attaches to the seller's history. If it stays clean through the exam window, the oracle releases the preimage and the seller is paid.
ideas.sponsor_use: XRPL Permissioned Domain/DEX plus Credentials carry the idea, because the product is that students cannot get in. An ordinary marketplace with a login is one leaked password from being scraped, and it cannot express 'only holders of this attestation can even hold this asset.' MPT Clawback and Lock let a pack be killed the instant it leaks. Conditional escrow ties seller payment to 'unleaked through the exam window.' Context.dev website-change monitoring is the leak oracle, a natural fit for its change-detection feature.
ideas.demo_moment: Adjunct A buys a 10-question Intro Stats midterm pack from Adjunct B, and the escrow shows as locked until the exam ends Thursday at 11:50. A student wallet tries to buy and is rejected by the Permissioned DEX for lacking a credential. Then the team posts question 7 to a mock 'study site' page. Context.dev change monitoring fires, the dashboard turns question 7 red ('leaked 2h before exam'), the escrow refunds Adjunct A, and B's remaining tokens of that pack get clawed back, all visible on the testnet explorer.
ideas.six_hour_buildability: Real: Credential issue and accept on testnet, an MPT with RequireAuth, Clawback and Lock flags, a conditional escrow with a server-held preimage oracle, and Context.dev monitoring of a page we control. Mocked: monitoring real Chegg (it is login-gated, so we say honestly that we watch a stand-in page or Quizlet public search), the department-chair issuer, and question-content encryption (simple AES with the key gated by token holdership). Key risk: Permissioned DEX trading of MPTs may not be supported or exposed in xrpl.js on testnet yet. The fallback is a credential-gated RequireAuth MPT plus a direct payment/escrow swap, which keeps the 'closed to students' story intact. Check amendment status in the first 30 minutes.
ideas.why_claude_wouldnt_default_to_this: The default campus-crypto ideas are student note-sharing, textbook resale, or anti-cheating surveillance. This flips the side (instructors trading among themselves) and identifies 'never been online' as the real perishable commodity. That makes a credential-gated closed market and clawback a structural need rather than decoration, and leak monitoring turns into a payment oracle instead of a cop.
